evidence: Both can hold. Example: a methodology structured as five parts, with intent at the top, communication at the base, and tasks, capability and quality between them. It is used to resolve tasks for a single agent, a multi-agent system, a company and a group of companies. Statement a describes the scale at which the methodology applies. Statement b describes its internal structure. Having 'tasks' as one of its parts fits with its purpose of resolving tasks. Nothing in b limits scale, and nothing in a limits the number or arrangement of parts.

Example: a methodology frames each task as a problem, applies the available capability to resolve it, and judges the result against quality criteria. It does this for one agent fixing a bug with its coding skill, judged by passing tests. It does the same for a group of companies meeting a joint contract with their combined resources, judged by the contract's quality criteria. That covers a's claim of resolving tasks at any scale and b's roles for task, capability and quality. Saying a methodology resolves tasks does not conflict with capability being the means. The methodology can be how that capability is organised and applied.

Statement a is about the range of scales the methodology covers. Statement b is about where tasks come from. Neither limits the other. Example: the environment keeps changing (a customer asks for a feature, a server runs short of capacity, a dependency needs patching). So tasks arise on request, out of need, and for maintenance. The same methodology then resolves such tasks for a single agent, a system of agents, one company, and a group of companies. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements address different things and do not conflict. Statement a says the methodology resolves tasks at every listed scale. Statement b says what organising tasks covers. A concrete example satisfies both: a methodology that resolves tasks for a single agent, a system of agents, a company, and a group of companies. At each scale it organises tasks by decomposing them into smaller tasks, mapping dependencies, prioritising, and classifying. Neither statement limits the other's scope or excludes anything the other requires.

Statement a concerns the scale at which the methodology resolves tasks. Statement b concerns which activities task management covers. Neither restricts the other. Example: a methodology is applied to fixing a defect, which counts as a task because it is a problem. It is used by a single agent and also by a group of companies. At each scale, managing the task means executing the fix, verifying the resulting artefact against its quality criteria at a point in time, and measuring the outcome. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

Example: the methodology is decomposition, a way of thinking for solving problems, and it is applied recursively. A group of companies takes on the task of launching a joint product. That task has an intent (serve a market), a capability (pooled budgets and staff) and a quality (agreed success criteria). It decomposes into one task per company. Each company task decomposes into tasks for a system of agents, and those decompose into tasks for single agents. Every subtask again has its own intent, capability and quality. The method resolves the task at each level: single agent, system of agents, company and group of companies. This satisfies a's claim that the methodology works at any scale and b's claims that decomposition is the methodology and that it is recursive. Statement a says nothing about how the methodology works, so b's account of it adds detail without conflict.

Example: a group of companies takes on a task with an agreed language and set of channels. Applying the methodology at that scale, it decomposes the task into one subtask per company, and each company then splits its part across teams and individual agents. Every split creates a new working group one level down. That group keeps the shared vocabulary and channels unchanged, and renegotiates its own milestones, deliverables with acceptance criteria, and fallback rules. The same methodology is used at every scale (a holds), and at each level the base is inherited while the local parts are adjusted (b holds). Statement b only describes what happens when a task is decomposed, so nothing in it stops a from covering every scale.

Example: one methodology is applied to two tasks. In the first, a single agent works with its operator. In the second, a group of companies works together. Each working group settles an agreement before starting, and the agreement includes exceptions, for instance: 'if the budget limit cannot be followed, refer the decision to the level above.' In each task, autonomy (resolving the task without referring decisions upward) is pursued as a goal, not imposed as a fixed standard. Its boundary is exactly where those exceptions require referral. The methodology resolves both tasks, which satisfies 'any scale' in a. Autonomy is a per-task goal bounded by the agreement's exceptions, which satisfies b. Neither statement forbids what the other requires.

Statement a only says the methodology can resolve tasks at every scale, from a single agent up to a group of companies. Statement b describes one specific task inside it, the comparison loop, and neither statement limits the other. Example: the methodology is used to resolve a single agent's problem, a multi-agent system's problem, a company's problem and a group of companies' problem. Within one of these uses, the comparison loop is delegated to a working group. Before starting, that group settles its own communication agreement (it will post results to a shared log). It then runs the loop with no outside intervention, and the user validates the result at the end. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement b is a question, not a claim. At most it presupposes that quality belongs either to the result or to the task–result relation, and a does not touch that presupposition. Example: a methodology resolves tasks for a single agent, a multi-agent system, a company and a group of companies, and quality is treated as a property of the relation between each task and its result (so quality is still what is pursued and the criterion of every judgement of the work). This satisfies a, and fits b's presupposition and the definitions. Choosing the other answer, quality as a property of the result, conflicts with a equally little.

Example: before starting work, a working group agrees how it will communicate (one shared channel, written decisions, a fixed format for status reports). That communication agreement is the base, and every other practice (task assignment, reviews, releases) is built on it, which satisfies b. The methodology also has a rule that every rule, including this one, is reviewed and may be revised at each retrospective. That rule covers the methodology itself and the communication agreement, so no part is exempt, which satisfies a. Being the foundation (b) does not require being exempt from the methodology (a). The foundation can itself be subject to review, so both hold together.

One scenario satisfies both. A methodology M contains rules, including 'a working group settles its agreement first,' and every rule of M, including the self-application rule, governs M itself and every agreement made under it. Alice and Bob form a working group for a task. The first thing they settle is their agreement: they will communicate through a shared written log. Then they start work. That agreement is subject to M's rules like everything else; for example, it can be reviewed and revised under M's procedures. M's own rules are bound by M as well. No part is exempt, so statement a holds. The agreement was settled first, before work began, so statement b holds. Neither statement requires anything to come before the agreement or to be exempt from the methodology.

Example: the methodology also governs the group's agreement. That agreement sets six components: shared English vocabulary (language), email and chat (channels), bullet summaries (format), weekly checkpoints (moments), named deliverables with acceptance criteria (commitments), and a rule to switch to phone if a channel fails (exceptions). Every component, including the exceptions clause, is itself subject to the methodology, so no part is exempt. 'Exception' is defined as what to do when part of the agreement cannot be followed. It is not an exemption from the methodology, so it does not clash with 'no part is exempt'.

Example: a working group settles its communication agreement before starting work. Under the methodology, that agreement is treated as an artefact: it is continuously monitored, and verified at points in time against its quality criteria, like any document or rule. The methodology's own rules are checked the same way, so no part is exempt (a). The agreement stays in force regardless of how much time passes or how often it is used (b). Not expiring is not an exemption from the methodology; ongoing monitoring is exactly how the methodology keeps applying to the agreement.

The two statements fit together. A says the methodology, including its own agreements, is never exempt from its own rules. B is one such rule, a failure-review-update cycle for agreements. Example: a methodology requires every artefact to be verified against its quality criteria, and that requirement applies to the methodology itself and to its agreements. Before work starts, a working group settles its communication agreement. When the agreement is verified, it fails because it names no channel for urgent issues. Since it failed, it is reviewed. The review finds a defect: the missing urgent-channel section is the part that failed. The agreement is then updated to add that channel. The methodology's own rules are also verified and reviewed in the same way, so no part is exempt. Every clause of A and B holds.

Example: a group maintains the methodology and decomposes the work, delegating a subtask (revising the exceptions section) to a subgroup. This creates a new working group. Following b, the subgroup inherits the parent's language and channels and renegotiates its own moments (weekly checkpoint), commitments (a draft, accepted on review) and exceptions. Following a, this is the methodology applied to its own work and agreements: the inheritance rule, the base and the local parts all fall under the methodology, so no part is exempt. Inheriting the base unchanged is itself an application of the methodology's rule, not an exemption from it. Only a strained reading of 'exempt' as 'not open to renegotiation' would make the inherited base look exempt, and a does not say that.

Per the supplied definition, an 'exception' is a fallback rule for when part of the agreement cannot be followed. It is not an exemption from the methodology, so b's exceptions do not clash with a's 'no part is exempt'. Example: a methodology governs a working group and is applied to itself and to the group's agreement, including that agreement's exception clauses, with nothing left outside it. The agreement says: 'If the agreed review step cannot be done, the task owner decides and logs the decision; if the budget would be exceeded, refer to the lead.' For every task, autonomy (resolving the task without referring decisions upward) is a goal, not a standard or a whole. The team decides everything itself except where the budget exception requires referral upward, so the exceptions set the boundary of autonomy. Both statements hold.

The two statements govern different things and fit together. Statement a says the methodology is subject to itself. Statement b lists the allowed responses to a diagnosis. Example satisfying both: a working group's own communication agreement, which is part of the methodology, fails a verification. It receives a diagnosis covering scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location. The group chooses one of the listed responses, for instance 'review the agreement', which examines the failed artefact. The response list itself is also open to verification, so no part is exempt. Every diagnosis, including those about the methodology's own parts, is answered only from the closed list in b.

Both hold if the escalation rule in b is one of the rules a applies to the methodology's own agreements. Example: group G, one level below task T, settles an agreement under methodology M. A defect measured below the threshold (tolerable) is fixed inside G. One measured above it (intolerable) goes up to T's level. The group that maintains M also works under a parent task, and the same rule governs its agreement, so no part of M is exempt. Every clause of a and b is satisfied. This depends on a level existing above M's own agreement; if M sat at the very top with an intolerable defect, escalation would have nowhere to go, but neither statement requires that case.

Example: a methodology includes rules for delegating tasks and for setting agreements, and those rules govern the methodology itself. The comparison loop is delegated under those rules. Before it starts, its group settles its own agreement as the methodology requires. It then runs without user intervention and the user validates the result at the end. Here the methodology still applies to the loop and to the loop's agreement, so nothing is exempt, and every clause of b also holds. 'Autonomous inside' means no user involvement during the work, not exemption from the methodology, so the two statements do not conflict.

Picture a five-layer methodology. At the bottom is communication, governed by the agreement the team settles before starting work. Tasks, capability and quality sit in the middle, and intent sits on top. This satisfies a: there are exactly five parts, with intent above, communication beneath, and the other three between them. It also satisfies b: communication is the bottom layer, and every other part ultimately rests on the agreement about communication, since being 'above' in a stack still means being built on what lies beneath. Neither statement says intent stands independently, and b's claim that everything is built on the agreement does not add a sixth part, because the agreement is what is settled about communication.

Example: a five-part methodology with intent at the top, the three middle parts (tasks, capability, quality) below it, and communication at the bottom. Intent is then above every other part, satisfying b's 'above everything' within the structure a describes. Each other part also takes its meaning from intent: tasks are the work intent states the purpose of, capability is the means to resolve those tasks, quality is the criteria for judging that work, and communication is the exchange that carries it. Statement b adds the claim that intent gives meaning to the rest; a is silent on this, so the addition does not conflict with a's layering.

Both can hold in one methodology. It has exactly five parts. Intent sits at the top and communication at the bottom. Tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Within that middle layer, a task is the problem to solve, capability is the means of solving it, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Statement b only gives the roles of the three middle parts named in a. It adds no part and says nothing about intent or communication, so the count and order in a are untouched. The definitions agree with b's roles: a task is, among other things, a problem; capability is the means to resolve a task; and quality is the criteria of every judgement of the work.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent sits at the top. Tasks, capability and quality sit in the middle layer. Communication is the bottom layer, and every relation between parts (intent to task, task to capability, work to quality) is carried out through the exchange of information, so communication is more than a channel. This satisfies a: five parts, intent above, communication beneath, the other three between. It also satisfies b: communication is foundational because it lies beneath, and cross-cutting because it is the medium of every relation. Being the bottom layer fits 'foundational', and being one of the five parts does not stop it from pervading the others.

There is no conflict because a counts the methodology's parts and b classifies its relations. Communication can be one part, the layer beneath, while also being the medium of every relation. Concrete example: a methodology has exactly five parts, with Intent at the top, Tasks, Capability and Quality in the middle, and Communication at the bottom. Its relations are all exchanges of information carried by the Communication layer. Distilling intent from one level to the next is downward communication. Verifying or reporting a result is upward communication. Consulting another party, which borrows its judgement, is lateral communication. Written know-how is communication deferred in time. Regulation is a judgement already made and communicated, as its definition states. No relation in the methodology is anything other than communication. This satisfies a's five parts in their stated arrangement and b's claim that every relation is communication, with each listed mapping.

Statement a lists the methodology's five parts, ordered top to bottom: intent above, then tasks, capability and quality in between, then communication beneath. Statement b lists properties of a communication; it does not add parts to the methodology. Concrete example: a methodology arranged in exactly those five layers, where each communication in the bottom layer has a fidelity, uses the group's shared language, has a direction, is either immediate or deferred, and goes to a person, an agent or the environment. Both sets have five items, but they are separate lists, so neither count limits the other. Nothing in either statement forbids what the other requires.

Statement a describes how the methodology's five parts are arranged: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Statement b says intent is set at each level of task decomposition. 'Above' in a places intent relative to the other parts. It does not limit intent to a single decomposition level. Concrete example: a methodology has exactly these five parts in that order. A project task is divided into subtasks, and those into sub-subtasks. At every one of these levels an intent statement is written saying what the work there is for. Each level's intent sits above the tasks, capability and quality applied at that level, with communication beneath. Every clause of a (five parts, the stated arrangement) and of b (intent set at each level) holds.

Statement a orders the five parts of the methodology: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Statement b says how intent carries across task-decomposition levels. These are different orderings, so they can coexist. Example: a methodology has exactly those five parts in that arrangement. Its top task, 'house a family', has the intent 'give the family safe shelter'. That task splits into the subtask 'lay the foundation', whose intent 'provide a stable base' is not a copy of the parent's intent. Instead it adds to it so that the parent's intent is fulfilled. Being 'above' as a part does not confine intent to the top level, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a methodology is laid out as five parts. Intent is at the top, communication is at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. This satisfies a. Under that methodology, a top task, 'make the service reliable', has the intent 'users can depend on it'. It is divided into one level of subtasks, such as 'add monitoring'. That subtask's intent, 'detect failures before users do', is derived from the higher intent. Some of the original is dropped, a specific target is added, and the purpose is restated in operational terms. That is distillation from level to level, which satisfies b. In a, 'above' places intent within the methodology's arrangement of parts. It is not a decomposition level, so it does not stop intent from being stated and distilled at every level.

Example: a methodology made of exactly five parts: intent on top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Verification is not a sixth part. It is a judgement made under quality, whose criteria include the intents. For a subtask's result, verification checks that the result meets the subtask's intent and that this intent still serves the intent of the parent task one level up. Statement a fixes the parts and their order. Statement b only describes what verification checks and never calls it a part, so both hold.

Statement a describes the structure: five parts, with intent on top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b only says that drift, the accumulation of small deviations across distillations, is able to empty the original intent of meaning. Neither statement limits the other. Example: a methodology has exactly those five parts in that arrangement. Its intent statement, 'what the work is for', is distilled several times. Each restatement shifts it slightly, and after enough rounds the original intent no longer conveys anything. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a describes how the methodology is structured: five parts, with intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b describes where tasks come from: a request, a need, or maintenance, because the environment changes. Neither restricts the other. Example: a methodology for running an online shop has exactly five parts. Its intent is 'serve customers reliably'. Its communication is the exchange of information with customers and staff. Between them sit tasks, capability (developers and tools) and quality (uptime and correctness criteria). Its tasks arise in three ways: a customer asks for a feature (request), rising traffic forces scaling (need), and a vendor library must be updated (maintenance). All three happen because customers and vendors outside the work keep changing it. This satisfies every clause of both statements, even if b is read as listing the only three ways a task can arise.

A methodology can have exactly five parts: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Within the tasks part, organising tasks covers decomposition (dividing a task into smaller tasks), dependencies, prioritisation and classification. Statement b describes sub-activities of one part. It adds no sixth part, so the count of five in a still holds. Nothing in either statement or the definitions rules this out.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent sits above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Managing the tasks part covers three activities: executing the work, verifying artefacts at points in time against criteria supplied by the quality part, and measuring progress. Statement b only describes what task management covers. It adds no sixth part, and neither statement says verification belongs exclusively to the quality part. Both statements hold in full.

Both can hold at once. Example: a problem-solving way of thinking called decomposition is the methodology. It is organised into five parts: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Applying it to a task splits that task into subtasks, and each subtask has its own intent, capability and quality, so the method repeats at every level. That satisfies (a) and every clause of (b). Calling the whole methodology 'decomposition' does not conflict with it having five parts, since a way of thinking can be made of parts. Recursion means only that the parts reappear at each subtask level. b's silence on whether subtasks have their own communication is not a prohibition.

The two statements cover different matters and can both hold. Statement a describes how the methodology is built: five parts, with intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b describes what happens to a working group's agreement when a task is decomposed and delegated. Nothing in a rules out new working groups or inherited agreements, and nothing in b adds or removes a part. Concrete example: a methodology has exactly five parts, ordered intent, then tasks, capability and quality, then communication. Task T is decomposed into subtasks, and subtask T1 is delegated. This forms a new working group one level down. That group keeps the parent's vocabulary and channels unchanged, since the base is inherited. It sets its own milestones, its own deliverables and how delivery is recognised, and its own exception rules, since the local parts are adjusted. Every clause of both statements is satisfied.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts. Intent sits above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality sit between them. Each task carries autonomy as one of its goals: the team should resolve the task without referring decisions upward. Autonomy is not counted as a sixth part, and it is not a standard; quality supplies the criteria. Before work starts, the group's agreement about communication includes exceptions, for example 'if a reporting step cannot be followed, refer the decision to the level above.' These exceptions mark where autonomy ends. Statement a lists the five parts, and b treats autonomy as a goal within tasks, with its limit set by the agreement's exceptions. Since autonomy is never claimed to be a part, the five-part count holds and every clause of both statements is satisfied.

Statement a fixes the methodology's structure: five parts, with intent above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b only classifies capability, the means available to resolve a task, as intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor. Nothing in a limits what kind of thing capability is. Example: a methodology with exactly those five parts arranged that way, where an executor's capability consists of their own skills (intrinsic) and an external toolset (extrinsic). Both statements hold together.

Example: a methodology with exactly five top-level parts, ordered intent (top), tasks, capability, quality, communication (bottom). Within the capability part, intrinsic capability (the executor's own means) consists of power, speed and context management. Statement a fixes the five top-level parts and their order. Statement b only breaks down a component of capability. Sub-components do not add top-level parts, so the count of five still holds and both statements are satisfied.

Statement a fixes the methodology's five parts: intent above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b adds no sixth part. It describes one kind of capability, extrinsic capability, as know-how, which the definitions call knowledge living outside the executor. Example: an organisation's methodology has exactly those five parts in that arrangement. Under capability (the means to resolve a task), it counts the person doing the work as the model. Its manuals, training courses and regulations count as know-how the organisation owns, kept outside that person. A regulation is a judgement already made and communicated, which fits with quality and communication remaining separate parts. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a methodology has exactly five parts, ordered with intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Separately, an external coding standard counts as normative know-how: it is knowledge held outside the executor. This standard adds no new means of resolving a task. Instead it forbids some of the available means, so it limits capability. Its rules also serve directly as criteria for judging the work, which connects it with quality. Statement b never claims that know-how is a part of the methodology, so the five-part count in a still holds. All clauses of both statements are satisfied.

Example: a methodology with exactly five parts, ordered intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Constraints, verification and monitoring are not separate parts. Each is derived from quality: constraints are limits drawn from quality, verification judges an artefact against its quality criteria, and monitoring is continuous verification. None of them is a starting point. This keeps the count of five in (a) and the derivation-only status in (b). The definitions support it: they define a constraint as derived from quality and verification as judged against quality criteria.

Both hold in this example. A methodology has exactly five parts: intent at the top, communication at the bottom, and tasks, capability and quality in between. Its quality part has the six attributes fitness for purpose, verifiability, performance, security, resilience and maintainability. Statement a fixes the number of methodology parts and their arrangement. Statement b only lists the attributes of one of those parts. Attributes of a part are not extra parts of the methodology, so the count of five is untouched, and nothing in the definition of Quality rules out these attributes.

The statements cover different things. (a) lists the methodology's five parts. (b) lists the responses available to a diagnosis. Example satisfying both: a methodology made of intent (top), communication (bottom), and tasks, capability and quality between them. Within it, a verification produces a diagnosis, graded by scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location. That diagnosis can be accepted, accepted with reservations, corrected, escalated, or answered by reviewing the agreement or the intent. Reviewing the agreement or intent fits the definition of review if they are treated as artefacts that failed a verification. Neither statement limits the other, and the five responses do not compete with the five parts.

Statement a lists the methodology's five parts: intent, communication, tasks, capability and quality. Statement b is a table of seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with an image and examples of slop. The definitions make figures kinds of defect, not parts of the methodology, so seven figures does not conflict with five parts. Concrete example: a methodology document organised into exactly those five parts, with intent at the top and communication at the bottom. Its quality part, which holds the criteria of judgement, contains b's table unchanged. Fit's slop 'an element not traceable to the intent' refers to a's intent part and so fits with it. Nothing in either statement excludes this arrangement.

Statement a describes the methodology's structure: intent above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Statement b describes one task within it. Example: a methodology has exactly those five parts. Under its tasks part, the comparison loop is delegated to an agent. Before work starts, the agent and user agree that the agent runs the loop autonomously and the user validates the result at the end. Per the definitions, that agreement is a matter of communication. Statement a sets no limit on what a task may contain, so a task with its own agreement does not change the five-part count. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

Statement b is a question and asserts nothing, so it adds no requirement that could conflict with a. Example: a methodology has exactly five parts, with intent on top, communication at the base, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Within that methodology someone asks whether quality belongs to the result or to the relation between task and result. Listing quality as one of the five parts does not settle that question, and the supplied definition of quality (what is pursued, achieved and applied; the criteria of judgement) fits either answer. Every clause of a holds and b is a legitimately open question.

Statement b is a question. It asserts nothing, though it presupposes that measurement has dimensions and that product quality can be separated from process quality. Statement a describes a five-part methodology: intent above, communication beneath, and tasks, capability and quality between them. Neither the presuppositions of b nor any clause of a excludes the other. Example satisfying both: a methodology has exactly those five parts in that arrangement. Within its quality part, measurement has dimensions such as conformance and timeliness. Product quality is judged against the delivered output's criteria, while process quality is judged against how the work was carried out. Reading b as making no claim, or as committing only to its presuppositions, gives the same result.

Example: a three-person working group first settles how its members will communicate. All later work, including tasks, reviews and decisions, is built on that agreement, so communication is the substrate (a). Every relation among the members, such as assigning, reviewing and trusting, is carried out through communication, so it is cross-cutting, foundational and the medium of every relation (b). Messages also travel along paths like email, so communication is a channel, but not only one. 'Substrate' and 'cross-cutting' are not exclusive: something can underlie everything and also run through every relation. 'Not only a channel' does not deny that it is a channel.

Example: three engineers form a working group. The first thing they settle is their agreement about communication: they will use English, a shared chat channel and a weekly sync. This happens before they start work, which matches the definition of 'agreement'. They then build their task plan, roles and deliverables on that agreement. So communication serves as the substrate and everything else rests on the agreement (statement a), and the agreement was the first thing settled when the group formed (statement b). Settling the agreement first is consistent with everything else being built on it, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: before starting work, a team settles its communication agreement. It fixes shared vocabulary and idiom (language), Slack and email (channels), and written briefs with a fixed template (format). It sets a weekly sync and milestone reviews (moments), who delivers what and how sign-off works (commitments), and a fallback of phoning the lead when a channel is down (exceptions). All later planning, building and review is organised on top of that agreement, so communication acts as the substrate. Statement b describes what the agreement contains. Statement a describes the agreement's foundational role. Neither limits the other.

Example: before starting, a working group settles its agreement on how it will communicate (channels, formats, who reports to whom). It then works through that agreement. A lead distils intent down to a team (downward). The team verifies an artefact and reports the result up (upward). A member consults a peer, borrowing their judgement (lateral). Lessons are written down as know-how for later readers (deferred in time). A regulation states what must and must not be done (a judgement already made). In this scenario communication is the substrate and the rest of the work is built on the agreement, satisfying a. Every listed relation is also a form of communication, satisfying b. Saying the relations are communication fits with communication being the substrate. 'Everything else' in a can cover the work built on those relations, so nothing conflicts.

Example: before starting work, a team settles a written communication agreement (channels, formats, response times). Every later document, rule and piece of code is produced under that agreement, so everything else is built on it, which satisfies a. The agreement is checkable, so it can be judged against quality criteria at fixed points (verification) and checked continuously (monitoring), in the same way the team's other artefacts are. It has no expiry date and stays in force however often it is used, which satisfies b. The only friction is that b's 'like any other artefact' could imply the agreement is a 'product of the work' even though it is settled before work starts. That is a question of b against the definitions, not a conflict with a. Read 'like' as 'handled in the same way as', or count the settling of the agreement as part of the work, and no clause fails.

Example: before starting work, a team settles its agreement on how it will communicate, and every later process and artefact is built on that agreement. This satisfies (a). Later, the agreement is checked against its quality criteria and fails. It is then reviewed, the review finds a defective clause, and the team updates the agreement. This satisfies (b). Being the foundation does not stop the agreement from being revised. The definition says it is settled before work starts, not that it can never change. (b) is also conditional, so it holds trivially if the agreement never fails a verification.

Statement a says communication is the foundation and the rest of the work rests on the agreement, which the definitions describe as what a working group settles about its communication before starting. Statement b only lists the properties a communication has. Example: before starting, a team agrees how it will communicate. It sets high fidelity, a shared vocabulary in plain English, two-way direction, deferred timing through tickets, and recipients that may be people, an automated agent or the environment (for example, a deployment). Every later task and decision is built on that agreement. Each message has fidelity, a shared language, a direction, a timing and a recipient, so b holds, and a holds too. b's list of properties says nothing that conflicts with a.

Example: a group's task is to build a report. Before work starts, the group settles its agreement: English with shared terms as the language, a shared chat channel, weekly checkpoints, each member's deliverables with sign-off as the recognition of delivery, and a rule to escalate to the lead if a checkpoint is missed. All of its work rests on this agreement, which satisfies a. The task is then decomposed and the data section is delegated to a sub-team, forming a new working group one level down. That sub-team keeps the same language and chat channel, so the base is inherited. It sets daily checkpoints, its own deliverables and its own escalation rule, so the local parts are adjusted. Its work in turn rests on this adjusted agreement. Statement a says what everything is built on, and b says how the agreement carries over across levels. Both clauses of b hold, and nothing in a forbids inheriting or adjusting the agreement.

Example: before starting work, a team sets an agreement about its communication. It covers daily status messages and an exception: 'if a status message cannot be sent, a member may settle decisions under $500 alone and must escalate anything larger.' Everything else, including roles, workflow and how tasks are run, is defined on top of that agreement, so communication is the substrate and the rest is built on the agreement (a). Each task aims for its owner to resolve it without referring decisions upward, so autonomy is a per-task goal. It is not a fixed standard or an overall property (b). How far that autonomy reaches is set by the exception clause, so its boundary comes from the agreement's exceptions (b). Autonomy being bounded by the agreement is itself an instance of 'built on the agreement', so the two statements support each other rather than conflict.

The two statements cover different subjects. (a) says communication is the foundation and everything rests on the agreement. (b) lists the allowed responses to a diagnosis. Example satisfying both: before starting, a team settles its communication conventions (channels, message formats, sign-off rules), and every later practice depends on that agreement. One of those practices is verification. When an artefact fails verification, the resulting diagnosis (scope, severity, urgency, tolerability, location) can be answered in only five ways: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. In one case the team accepts with reservations; in another it reviews the agreement. Reviewing the agreement does not conflict with (a): a foundation can still be examined after a failure and revised.

Example: before starting, a working group settles its communication agreement: daily written status reports, and a defect threshold where latency of 200 ms or more counts as intolerable. All later work rests on this agreement, including the task decomposition, the threshold and the escalation route. That satisfies (a): communication is the substrate and everything else is built on the agreement. The task 'build service' sits one level above its subtasks 'API' and 'database'. The API team measures a defect at 150 ms. It is below the threshold, so it is tolerable within the agreement, and the API team resolves it at its own level. A second defect measures 400 ms. It is intolerable, so the team escalates it to the 'build service' level. The team's autonomy therefore covers exactly the tolerable defects, which satisfies (b). Statement (b) describes how work runs inside the agreement that (a) names as the foundation, so no clause conflicts.

Example: a user and an agent first settle how they will communicate, including what gets reported, when, and in what format. Everything they do afterwards rests on that agreement, which satisfies a. Under it, the user delegates a comparison loop. Before the loop starts, the agent and its sub-workers settle their own agreement on how they exchange comparison results. The loop then runs with no user input until the end, when the user reviews and approves the outcome, which satisfies b. 'Autonomous inside' only means the user does not intervene during the loop. It does not mean the loop lacks communication or an agreement, so the loop is still built on agreement. Its 'own agreement' can sit inside, and depend on, the main agreement, so 'everything is built on the agreement' still holds.

The two statements make claims about different things, so both can hold. a ranks intent (a statement of what work is for) above everything and makes it the source of meaning. b classifies the methodology's relations as kinds of communication. Concrete example: a project's top-level intent is 'deliver a safe bridge', and every other element takes its meaning from that intent. That intent is distilled downward to a team's intent ('design the deck to load spec'), which is downward communication. Verification results are reported upward to whoever holds the intent. Engineers consult a peer for judgement, which is lateral. Written design guides carry know-how deferred in time. Building codes act as regulation, a judgement already made and communicated. Every relation is communication (b), and all of them serve and take meaning from the intent (a). Intent is a statement, not a relation, so b's 'every relation is communication' does not compete with a's 'intent is above everything'. Downward distillation of intent also fits intent being at the top.

Example: a project's top task has the intent 'reduce customer churn'. It splits into subtasks such as 'redesign onboarding' and 'improve support response'. Each subtask has its own intent stating what it is for: 'help new users succeed early' and 'resolve problems before customers leave'. Every level therefore has an intent set (b). The top intent sits above all tasks and lower intents and gives them their meaning (a). Statement a says intent is paramount and gives meaning to everything; it does not say intent exists only at the top. So intents at each level, all serving the overarching one, satisfy both statements.

Example: the top task has the intent 'give the village safe drinking water.' A subtask, 'dig a well,' has the intent 'provide reliable access to groundwater.' This lower intent does not copy the higher one word for word, so inheritance is non-strict. It adds what the well is for, so it complements the higher intent. It serves the village goal, so it fulfils it, which satisfies b. In each task, the intent ranks above the plans, methods and actions and gives them their purpose; for instance, the well's depth and location matter only because of what the well is for. The top intent also gives meaning to the subtask's intent, so intent stays above everything and gives meaning to everything else, which satisfies a. This also holds if a refers to the single top-level intent, because lower intents exist to fulfil it.

Example: a project's top task has the intent 'make city cycling safe.' Its subtask's intent is derived from it as 'cut bike-lane collisions by 30%.' That derivation drops the parts about other risks (something lost), adds a numeric target (something added), and turns the aim into traffic-engineering terms (something translated). So intent is distilled from level to level, as b requires. The top intent sits above every task and plan, and it gives meaning to everything else, including the derived lower-level intents and the work done under them, as a requires. Even on the reading where 'above everything' means intent outranks plans and methods at every level, each level's distilled intent still governs and gives meaning to the work at that level. A lower level adding content does not stop the higher intent from giving it meaning, because a does not say intent is the only source of meaning. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a project's top intent is 'reduce customer churn'. A subtask one level down has the intent 'build a cancellation survey'. Verification of the survey, judged against criteria drawn from that intent, checks two things: that the survey fulfils its own intent, and that this intent still serves churn reduction. Intent, ending in the top-level one, sits above every artefact, criterion and check and gives each its meaning, which satisfies a. Verification is a judgement made against intents, which satisfies b. A says intent is above 'everything else', meaning things other than intent. Lower-level intents serving higher ones is therefore an ordering among intents and does not conflict with a.

The answer depends on how 'above everything' in a is read. Reading 1 (priority or role): a ranks intent as the governing standard and the source of meaning for everything else. On this reading the pair is compatible. Example: in a pipeline, the intent statement ranks first and every distillation is judged against it, yet small accumulated deviations leave the original intent statement hollow, as b allows. a speaks of 'everything else', so it says nothing about intent's own meaning, and b concerns the 'original' intent, which can differ from the intent currently in force. Reading 2 (supremacy): a means nothing can override or diminish intent, and intent always gives meaning. Drift emptying intent of meaning would then be something placed over intent, and an emptied intent could not give meaning to anything. On this reading the pair is a contradiction. The pair alone does not settle which reading is meant.

Example: a house project whose intent, 'provide safe shelter', ranks above everything else and gives meaning to all of it, including how the work is organized. The method used is decomposition, a way of thinking about the problem. The project splits into tasks such as foundation and walls. Each task has its own intent (e.g., 'carry the load'), its own capability (the crew and tools available) and its own quality (load criteria). Each task can split again, so the method is recursive. Every sub-intent takes its meaning from the top intent, so intent stays above everything. Statement a ranks intent above all; statement b only names decomposition as the method and says each task has an intent. Calling decomposition 'the methodology' does not rank it above intent, and having many task-level intents fits with intent as the governing category. Every clause of both statements holds.

Both can hold at once. Example: a team defines the intent as 'this report is for helping managers decide on the budget', and the intent gives meaning to every other part of the work. A verification produces a diagnosis (scope, severity, urgency, tolerability, location), and the team chooses one of the five listed responses, for instance reviewing the intent. Under the supplied definition, review is only an examination of an artefact after it fails a verification. Examining the intent does not displace it or deny its primacy, so the intent still sits above everything and gives meaning to the rest. Statement a does not forbid examining the intent, and statement b only lists the possible responses without ranking them above the intent.

Statement b is a defect classification table. It ranks nothing above intent. Its 'fit' row counts 'an element not traceable to the intent' as slop, which actually depends on intent being primary, as a says. Example satisfying both: a work opens with an intent statement that governs every element and gives each its meaning. Its quality checks label defects exactly as the table does: an element in the wrong language is 'form' slop; one that contradicts another or cannot be traced to the intent is 'fit' slop; one said twice is 'economy' slop; an undefined term is 'completeness' slop; a term used before its definition is 'order' slop; a term with two meanings or a sentence with two readings is 'sharpness' slop; a claim of verification without evidence is 'truthfulness' slop. Nothing in this setup breaks either statement.

Statement a gives the roles of task, capability and quality. Statement b says where tasks come from and why. Neither excludes the other. Example: a library's environment keeps changing, because users ask for things and dependencies get updated, so the environment is 'alive'. A user requests an export feature, so the task arises on request. A dependency is deprecated and must be replaced, so a task arises for maintenance. Each task is a problem to solve. The team's skills and tools are the capability used to resolve it. The finished work is judged against quality criteria such as correctness and performance. Every clause of a and b holds in this example, and it matches the supplied definitions: a task is a problem, capability is the means, quality is the criteria for judgement, and the environment is what can change the work.

Example: a team must fix a login failure. That task is the problem. The developers' skills and tools are the capability used to resolve it. Passing tests and security standards are the quality criteria the work is judged against, which satisfies (a). Organising the work splits the fix into subtasks (decomposition), notes that the patch must come before redeployment (dependencies), ranks it above cosmetic fixes (prioritisation) and labels it a security bug (classification), which satisfies (b). Statement (a) describes what tasks, capability and quality are. Statement (b) lists what organising tasks covers. Neither restricts the other.

The statements are compatible. A says what tasks, capability and quality are; B says what managing tasks includes. Example: a bug-fix task is the problem, the developer's skills and tools are the capability used to resolve it, and the acceptance criteria are the quality the work is judged against. Managing that task covers executing the fix, verifying the patched code against its quality criteria at a point in time, and measuring results such as test pass rates. Every clause of both statements holds, and nothing in either rules out the other.

Example: the task 'build a shed' is the problem. Its capability (a carpenter and tools) is the means to resolve it, and its quality (it stands level and keeps out rain) is what the work is judged against. Thinking through the problem by decomposition splits it into subtasks such as 'pour the foundation'. That subtask has its own intent (support the shed), its own capability (a concrete crew) and its own quality (cured flat within tolerance). It is again a problem resolved by capability and judged against quality. Statement a assigns roles to task, capability and quality. Statement b adds that tasks decompose recursively, with each subtask carrying the same elements. Nothing in either statement conflicts with the other.

The statements cover different things: a gives the roles of task, capability and quality, and b describes how the agreement carries across decomposition levels. Neither excludes the other. Example: the task 'launch a website' is a problem. The capability to resolve it is a developer team with its tools. The work is judged against quality criteria such as accessibility and load time. The task is decomposed, and 'build the checkout page' is delegated to a sub-team, forming a new working group one level down. That group inherits the base of the agreement: shared English, the project's domain vocabulary and the existing chat and ticket channels. It renegotiates the local parts: a weekly checkpoint (moment), delivery of a tested checkout page accepted on passing payment tests (commitment), and escalation to the parent lead if the payment API is unavailable (exception). Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a team's communication agreement includes an exception: 'if the reviewer is unavailable, the developer may merge after tests pass and notify the lead; any other deviation goes to the lead.' Each task, such as fixing a bug, is the problem. The developer's skills and tools are the capability used to resolve it. The work is judged against quality criteria such as correctness and test coverage. For each task, one goal is that the developer resolves it without referring decisions upward; this is autonomy. Autonomy is not one of the judging criteria, so it is not a standard, and it is not treated as a whole. Its boundary is exactly what that exception permits. Statement a assigns the standard role to quality only. Pursuing a goal does not make that goal the standard, so the two statements do not clash.

Example: the task is to fix a leaking pipe, which is the problem. The executor is a plumber. The capability is the plumber's own skill (intrinsic to the executor) plus a borrowed wrench (extrinsic to the executor). Both are means available to resolve the task. The quality is a watertight, code-compliant seal, and the work is judged against it. Statement a holds: the task is the problem, capability is the means and quality is the standard of judgement. Statement b holds: each capability is either intrinsic or extrinsic to the executor. This works whether b's 'or' is read as inclusive or exclusive, because each item falls on exactly one side. Statement a says nothing about where capability resides, so b only adds detail.

Example: an executor is given a bug-fixing task, which is the problem. Its capability is the means of resolving it. The intrinsic part of that capability consists of power (its strength and the effort it applies), speed (fixing several modules in parallel) and context management (choosing which code to keep in mind at each step). The fix is then judged against quality criteria such as correctness. Statement a says what role capability plays (the means), and statement b says what intrinsic capability is made of. These two claims do not conflict.

Example: an organisation assigns a model a task, such as resolving a customer complaint, which is the problem. The model draws on the organisation's documents, courses and regulations, which is extrinsic capability: know-how that sits outside the model and belongs to the organisation. These are the means of resolution. The finished work is then judged against quality criteria. This example satisfies statement a (task as problem, capability as means, quality as the standard of judgement) and statement b (extrinsic capability as know-how; person as model; documents, courses and regulations as organisational know-how). A regulation is a judgement already made and passed on, but it serves here as a means. It does not replace quality as the standard, so the two statements do not clash.

Example: the task is designing a bridge, which is the problem to solve. Capability is the engineers, tools and methods available to solve it. Quality is the safety and performance criteria the design is judged against. That satisfies a. Normative know-how is the external building code, which lives outside the executor. It adds no new means; instead it rules out some methods the engineers could otherwise use, so it limits capability. Its rules also directly set the quality criteria. That satisfies b. Statement a never says capability is unconstrained or that quality is unrelated to know-how, so both statements hold together.

Example: the task (the problem) is that a login page fails. The capability (the means) is a developer with access to the code. Quality, the criterion the work is judged against, is that valid logins succeed within 2 seconds. The constraint 'response must stay under 2 s' is derived from that quality. Verification is a release-time test of the build against the quality criteria. Monitoring is continuous running of the same check. None of the constraint, verification or monitoring originates independently; each traces back to quality. Every clause of a and b holds, and the supplied definitions say the same thing (constraint derived from quality; verification against quality criteria; monitoring as continuous verification).

Statement a gives roles: a task is the problem, capability is the means of resolving it, and quality is the standard the work is judged against. Statement b lists quality's attributes. Nothing conflicts, because b only details what a's quality standard consists of. Example: the task is to fix a failing payment service. The capability is an engineer with the codebase and test tools. The resulting work is judged against quality, meaning whether it is fit for purpose, verifiable, performant, secure, resilient and maintainable. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a gives general roles: a task is the problem, capability resolves it, and quality is the standard it is judged against. Statement b describes one particular task: the comparison loop is delegated, has its own agreement, runs autonomously inside, and is validated by the user at the end. The two fit together. Concrete example: an agent is delegated the comparison loop. Before starting, the agent and the user agree how they will communicate: the agent reports only once, at the end. The loop is the problem to solve. The agent's comparison tools and procedures are the capability used to solve it. The agent runs the loop without consulting the user. At the end, the user validates the result against stated quality criteria, such as accuracy and completeness of the comparison. This satisfies every clause of a and of b. User validation is simply an act of judging the work against quality, and having an agreement and autonomy is extra detail that a neither requires nor forbids.

Statement b is a question, so it asserts nothing. At most it presupposes that quality belongs either to the result or to the relation between task and result. Statement a, read with the definitions, makes quality the criteria the work is judged against, which are also pursued and achieved in the work. That fits the 'relation' option, and even the 'result' option if quality is achieved in the result. Example: the task is to build a bridge that carries 10 tonnes. The capability is the engineering team and materials. The quality is how well the finished bridge meets the 10-tonne requirement, which is the standard used to judge the work. Here quality is a relation between task and result, so b's presupposition holds and every clause of a holds.

b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. Its presuppositions are that measurement has dimensions and that product quality can be separated from process quality. Both can hold together with a. Example: the task is a software module that fails under load (the problem). The team's skills and tools are the capability used to fix it. The work is judged against quality criteria measured along dimensions such as correctness, performance and timeliness. Product quality (whether the delivered module meets those criteria) is assessed separately from process quality (whether testing and review procedures were followed). Each part of a holds, and every presupposition of b is satisfied.

Example: a working group conducts every relation through the exchange of information, so communication is foundational and more than a channel. Before starting work, it settles an agreement about that communication with exactly six components: a shared vocabulary (language), paths for information (channels), the shape of exchanges (format), milestones and checkpoints (moments), promised deliverables and how they are recognised (commitments), and what to do when a rule can't be followed (exceptions). Statement a only says communication is more than a channel; it does not stop channels from being one of the agreement's six components. Both statements hold.

Example: a methodology whose only relations are the five listed, each carried out entirely as an exchange of information. Distilling intent passes downward from a level to the one below. Verifying or reporting a result passes upward. Consulting another borrows a peer's judgement laterally. Written know-how is information exchanged with a later reader. Regulation communicates a judgement already made. Here every relation is communication, which satisfies b. Communication is also the medium of every relation and spans all directions and times, so it is cross-cutting and foundational and not merely one path among others, which satisfies a. Saying a relation 'is' communication (b) and that communication is its 'medium' (a) can both be true when each relation consists of, and takes place through, an exchange of information. b's table adds detail that a does not mention, which is not a conflict.

Statement a says what role communication plays: it underlies every relation and is more than a channel. Statement b lists the properties a single communication has. Neither excludes the other. Concrete example: in a working group, every relation is carried by communications, so communication is the medium of each relation and not just the path it travels. One such communication is a developer's code-review comment to a reviewer. It has high fidelity, uses the group's shared technical English, runs from developer to reviewer, is deferred because it is read later, and its recipient is a person. A second is a deploy script's message to the environment, which is immediate and has the environment as recipient. Both statements hold in this scenario.

Example: a team's task (a problem) is decomposed, and one subtask is delegated to a new subgroup. Every relation in both groups, whether between members or between parent and subgroup, is carried by exchanging information. That satisfies a: communication is the medium of every relation. Communication here also covers shared language, moments, commitments and exceptions, so it is more than a channel. Before starting, the subgroup settles its agreement (b). It inherits the parent's vocabulary and idiom and the same chat and repository channels. It renegotiates its own checkpoint cadence, what each member delivers and how delivery is recognised, and what to do when a deadline cannot be met. The same happens at each further level. Neither statement limits the other. a makes no claim about how agreements change across levels, and b's structuring of the agreement assumes communication underlies each working group's relations, which fits a.

Statement a fixes when the agreement is settled: first, when the group forms. Statement b fixes what it contains: six components. These do not conflict. Example: three parties form a working group for a task. Before doing anything else, and before starting work, they settle their communication agreement. It covers language (shared vocabulary and idiom), channels (e.g. a chat thread and email), format (shape of exchanges), moments (a weekly cadence plus milestone checkpoints), commitments (what each party delivers and how delivery is recognised) and exceptions (what to do if a part cannot be followed). The agreement is the first thing settled and has exactly those six components, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a working group forms and, before anything else, settles its communication agreement. This satisfies (a). The agreement can be checked, so it is treated as an artefact. Throughout the task it is continuously verified against its quality criteria, which is monitoring, and it stays in force however long it lasts and however often it is used. This satisfies (b). Being settled first does not conflict with being monitored later, and monitoring does not imply expiry. One minor tension: the definitions describe artefacts as products of 'the work', while the agreement is settled before work starts. However, (b) only requires that the agreement be monitored and verified like other artefacts, which this example does.

Example: a working group forms, and the first thing it settles is its communication agreement, before starting work (satisfies a). Later the agreement fails a verification, so it is reviewed. The review finds a defect, a part that failed the verification, and the agreement is updated (satisfies b). Updating the agreement later does not conflict with it being the first thing settled at formation.

Example: a product team forms and, before any work, settles its agreement: English with shared project terms, a chat channel and a tracker, a weekly sync, a working prototype accepted at a demo, and escalation to the lead if the sync is missed. It then splits the task and delegates the payment module to a new sub-team. That sub-team's first act is to settle its own agreement. It keeps the same language and channels, and adjusts the local parts: daily check-ins, the module counts as delivered once integration tests pass, and the parent team's lead is contacted if a check-in fails. Both groups settle their agreement first (a). At the new level the base is inherited and the local parts are adjusted (b). Taking on inherited parts can itself be part of settling the agreement, so the two statements do not conflict.

Example: a working group forms to fix a software bug. The first thing it settles is its agreement on communication: daily updates in a shared channel. The agreement includes one exception: if an update cannot be given or a fix would change the public interface, the decision is referred to the team lead. Starting work comes later. For this task, the group aims to resolve as much as it can without referring decisions upward. That autonomy is a goal for this task, not a fixed standard or a property of the whole organization. Its boundary is exactly the cases named in the agreement's exception. This satisfies a (the agreement is settled first, at formation) and every clause of b (autonomy is a per-task goal, not a standard or whole, bounded by the agreement's exceptions). The two statements address different matters and fit together consistently.

Example: a working group forms, and the first thing it settles is its agreement on how it will communicate. It then starts work. Later a piece of its work fails a verification, and the diagnosis records scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location. The group's available responses are accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Review means examining an artefact after a failed verification, and the agreement is such an artefact. Statement a fixes when the agreement is first settled. Statement b lists the responses that come after a diagnosis. They concern different points in time, so both hold.

Statement a sets when the agreement is settled: first, when the group forms. Statement b sets how defects within that agreement are handled afterwards. Example: a working group forms for a task. Before doing anything else it settles its agreement on communication formats and a latency threshold. Later, a message delay is measured at 50 ms against a 100 ms threshold, so it is tolerable and the group resolves it itself. Another delay measures 300 ms, which is intolerable, so the group escalates it to the task one step up. Here the agreement was settled first, tolerable defects stay at the group's level, intolerable ones go up, and tolerability marks where the group's autonomy ends. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: when the comparison loop is delegated, its working group (say, two agents) forms. The first thing it does is settle its own agreement about how it will communicate. That satisfies a, and also b's 'its own agreement', since an agreement is settled before work starts. The agents then run the loop without outside intervention, which makes it autonomous inside. At the end the user reviews and approves the result. Statement a only fixes the order in which a group settles things. Nothing in b conflicts with settling the agreement first, so both statements hold.

Example: before starting, a working group settles an agreement covering a shared glossary and idiom (language), chat and email (channels), a written status template (format), weekly syncs and milestone reviews (moments), deliverables with acceptance criteria (commitments) and an escalation procedure for when a rule cannot be followed (exceptions). The group checks the agreement against its quality criteria at each sync and keeps checking it continuously, as it does with its documents and code. The agreement has no end date and stays in force however often it is used. This satisfies both statements. Statement a fixes the agreement's contents; statement b concerns how it is checked and that it lasts. Neither limits the other. The agreement is settled before work begins, but it can still be checked, so it can reasonably count as an artefact.

Example: a working group's agreement has exactly six components. Language is English with a shared glossary. Channel is a team chat. Format is written summaries. Moments are a weekly checkpoint. Commitments are each member's deliverables. Exceptions say to fall back to email if chat is down. The agreement fails a verification because the commitments component does not say how delivery is recognised, so it is reviewed. The review finds that component is a defect, and the agreement is updated by adding acceptance criteria to commitments. It still has the same six components. Statement a fixes the structure; statement b only sets conditional review and update steps, which can change a component's content without changing the component list, so every clause of both holds.

The two statements describe different things. (a) lists the six components of an agreement, which the definitions say is what a working group settles about its communication before work starts. (b) lists five properties of a single communication, which the definitions say is an exchange of information. Neither count limits the other, and overlapping terms such as language and timing versus moments are not required to be distinct or exclusive. Example: a team's agreement has six components: language (shared English plus a project glossary), channels (a chat tool and email), format (written status summaries), moments (a weekly checkpoint), commitments (deliver a report, recognised by the lead's sign-off) and exceptions (escalate to the lead if a checkpoint is missed). Under that agreement, one communication is a chat message from the lead to a member. It has high fidelity, uses the shared language, flows lead-to-member, is deferred and goes to a person. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a working group's agreement covers all six components: a shared vocabulary, a chat channel plus a repository, structured status reports, weekly checkpoints, a promised deliverable with acceptance tests, and an escalation rule. The task is decomposed and a subtask is delegated, which forms a new working group one level down. That group inherits the vocabulary and the channels. It adjusts its own moments (daily checkpoints), commitments (a smaller deliverable with its own tests) and exceptions. It also keeps the report format. This satisfies a, since the agreement still has six components, and it satisfies b, since the base is inherited and the local parts are adjusted at each level. b does not mention format, but it does not say format is excluded, and it does not claim the agreement has only five components, so the omission creates no conflict.

Example: a working group's agreement lists six components: shared vocabulary (language), chat and email (channels), a written-update template (format), weekly check-ins (moments), named deliverables with acceptance criteria (commitments), and exceptions. The exceptions component says: 'If a deadline or channel cannot be followed, refer the decision to the team lead; otherwise resolve it yourself.' For every task, the goal is that the member resolves it without escalating. Autonomy is treated as that per-task goal, not as a standard or a whole. The exceptions clause sets where autonomy ends, because it names when decisions go to the level above. Statement a fixes six components, including exceptions. Statement b only gives the exceptions component an extra role and classifies autonomy. It does not add a seventh component or remove one, so every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a lists the parts of the agreement. Statement b lists the possible responses to a diagnosis. Nothing in one limits the other. Example: a working group's agreement has exactly six components: a shared glossary and idiom (language), chat and email (channels), report templates (format), a weekly checkpoint (moments), named deliverables with acceptance criteria (commitments), and a fallback procedure for when the agreement can't be followed (exceptions). Later, a verification produces a diagnosis giving scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location. The group's possible responses are exactly accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Here it chooses to review the agreement, which fits the definition of review as examining an artefact after it fails a verification. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

Example: a working group settles an agreement with exactly six components: a shared glossary in plain English (language), chat and email (channels), structured status reports (format), weekly check-ins and milestone reviews (moments), deliverables each recognised by an acceptance test (commitments), and an exceptions clause. That clause says each defect is measured against a threshold. Defects within the threshold are tolerable and are resolved at the task's own level. Defects beyond it are escalated to the level above. So a party acts autonomously exactly up to the tolerability boundary. Statement b's rule sits inside the exceptions component, so the agreement still has six components and both statements hold.

The two statements cover different subjects and share no requirement that could clash. Statement a lists the six components of an agreement. Statement b is a table of seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with an image and an example of slop. Example satisfying both: a working group settles an agreement before starting work. It covers (1) language: a shared vocabulary and idiom, e.g. English plus the methodology's defined terms; (2) channels, e.g. a team chat and email; (3) format, e.g. structured status notes; (4) moments, e.g. a weekly cadence and milestone reviews; (5) commitments, e.g. each party delivers its section, recognised by sign-off; (6) exceptions, e.g. escalate to the lead when a part cannot be followed. Separately, the same methodology checks artefacts against the seven figures in b's table. Typical slop includes an element in the wrong language (form), the same thing said twice (economy), or a verification claim without evidence (truthfulness). Nothing in b limits or changes the number or identity of the agreement's components, so both statements hold at once.

Statement a says what any agreement contains. Statement b says the comparison loop has its own agreement and is autonomous until a final user validation. A concrete example satisfies both. The working group delegated the comparison loop settles six components before starting. Language: a shared comparison vocabulary. Channels: one path for reporting back to the user. Format: a final comparison report. Moments: no intermediate checkpoints with the user, only an end-of-loop checkpoint, so the loop is autonomous inside. Commitments: deliver the report, with delivery recognised when the user validates it at the end. Exceptions: if inputs are unavailable, stop and report at the checkpoint. This agreement has all six components, as a requires, and meets every clause of b.

Example: a working group writes an agreement before starting work, e.g. 'results are reported upward weekly and peers are consulted laterally.' The agreement is a checkable document, so it counts as an artefact. It is monitored, meaning continuously verified against its quality criteria, the same way as any other artefact, and it stays in force without expiring through time or use. Every relation in the methodology is still communication. Distilling intent is downward. Verifying or reporting a result, including verifying the agreement itself, is upward. Consulting is lateral. Written know-how, including the agreement, is communication deferred in time. Regulation is a judgement already made. Nothing in (a) forbids artefacts from being verified or from being permanent, and nothing in (b) adds a relation that falls outside communication, so both statements hold together.

Example: a working group settles its agreement on how it will communicate before starting work. A verification checks the agreement against its quality criteria and the result is reported upward. The agreement fails, so it is reviewed by consulting another party laterally. The review finds a defect, a part that failed the verification, and the agreement is updated. Every relation used is communication: upward for verifying and reporting, lateral for consulting. That satisfies (a). Fail-then-review and defect-then-update satisfy (b). Statement (a) only classifies relations as communication, and (b) only adds conditional steps, so nothing clashes.

Statement a says every relation in the methodology is a communication and labels each one. Statement b lists the properties any communication has. These fit together: a's labels downward, upward and lateral are values of b's 'direction', and 'deferred in time' is a value of b's 'timing'. Concrete example: a lead distils intent downward to a person (shared idiom, some fidelity loss, immediate). A tester reports a verification result upward to the lead (immediate).
