The statements cover different steps. (a) says what a verification outputs: a graded diagnosis rather than a binary verdict. (b) lists how someone may respond to that diagnosis. 'Accept' in (b) is a response to the diagnosis, not the verification's output, so it does not reintroduce a yes/no result. Example: a report is verified against its quality criteria. The verification returns a diagnosis: scope is section 3, severity is minor, urgency is low, the issue is tolerable, and the location is paragraph 2. The team then chooses one of the listed responses, 'accept with reservations'. The verification returned a diagnosis (satisfying a), and the response came from the permitted list (satisfying b).

Statement a is about what a verification outputs: a graded diagnosis (scope, severity, urgency, tolerability, location) rather than a pass or fail. Statement b is a table that classifies kinds of slop under each figure, with an image and concrete examples for each. b never says a verification returns yes or no, so the two do not conflict. Example: an artefact has element E3, which uses the term 'tolerance' without defining it. By b, that is completeness slop. A verification then reports a diagnosis: scope one term, severity low, urgency low, tolerable, location E3. That satisfies a's requirement of a diagnosis instead of a yes or no. If the same artefact also says 'verified' with no supporting evidence, b counts that as truthfulness slop, and it would appear as another graded finding in the same diagnosis. Every row of b's mapping and a's clause hold together.

Statement b moves only the contradiction and redundancy judgement to formalisation. It does not stop verification from returning a graded result. Example: an artefact's elements E1 to E40 are written as description-logic axioms, which are decidable. At formalisation a reasoner runs once and records two minimal unsatisfiable subsets, {E3,E7} and {E7,E9,E12}, and records that E20 is entailed by the rest, so E20 is redundant. A later verification against the artefact's quality criteria reads these records and returns a diagnosis rather than a yes or no. Scope: 2 contradictions and 1 redundancy among 40 elements. Severity: high for the contradictions, low for the redundancy. Urgency: fix the contradictions before release. Tolerability: the contradictions are not tolerable, the redundancy is. Location: E3, E7, E9, E12 and E20. All clauses of a and b hold. The decidable logic gives exact per-check answers, and the counts and locations feed the graded diagnosis. Nothing in b requires the verification outcome itself to be binary.

Statement a sets the form of the artefact-level output: a verification returns a graded diagnosis. Statement b governs the inputs to that output: binary decisions per run, and a defect, no-defect or escalated outcome per element. Neither statement says the verification itself outputs a yes or a no. Example: an artefact has elements E1 and E2, and the panel is models M1 and M2, each giving one run per element with no schema failures and no missing runs. For E1, both runs return p = 0.92, and SLP.24 decides each as yes, so E1 is a defect. For E2, both runs return p = 0.05, decided no, so E2 has no defect. The verification is complete and returns a diagnosis: scope one element, severity moderate, urgency low, tolerable, location E1. Every clause of a and b holds. One assumption: SLP.24's content is not given, so this example assumes it can decide those p values as yes and no respectively.

The two statements describe different outputs. Statement a is about what a verification as a whole returns: a diagnosis, not a yes or no. Statement b is about the per-pair reply from the judge model (contradiction, compatible or refer). It treats that reply as a component of a verification, since a bad reply 'leaves the verification incomplete'. So the per-pair reply is not the verification's own result, and it is three-valued with reasons anyway. Example: the judge (anthropic/claude-opus-5.5, temperature 0, template identified by its SHA-256 hash) receives elements E1 and E2, which share the term 'Verification', each pair sent alone with the relevant glossary definitions. It replies 'contradiction' and names the clashing requirements. Another pair gets 'refer', which is escalated to the user. All replies pass the schema and there is no transport failure. The verification then returns a diagnosis: scope = E1/E2 and the referred pair; severity = high; urgency = before release; tolerability = not tolerable; location = E1, E2. That diagnosis is not a yes or no, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example: a verification of artefact D against its criteria returns a diagnosis (scope: section 2; severity: medium; urgency: low; tolerable; location: line 40), not a pass/fail. That judgement is recorded with input hash H1, template hash T1, models M1 and M2, N=5 and k=3. A later verification reads the record, finds H1 and T1 unchanged, does not judge again, and returns the recorded diagnosis. When D is edited, its hash becomes H2, so the next verification judges again and returns a new diagnosis. Statement a fixes only the form of the output (a graded diagnosis). Statement b governs recording and when re-judgement happens. Reusing a cached diagnosis still returns a diagnosis. The only nuance is that the definition calls a verification a 'point-in-time judgement', and a cache hit reuses an earlier judgement. That does not stop either statement from holding.

Statement a lists the permitted responses to a diagnosis. Statement b says which level handles a diagnosis, depending on its tolerability. Example satisfying both: a working group verifies its task and gets two diagnoses. Diagnosis 1 measures within the agreement's threshold, so it is tolerable. The group resolves it at its own level by accepting it with reservations (or correcting it), without referring to the level above. Diagnosis 2 exceeds the threshold, so it is not tolerable. The group escalates it to the level above. Every response used is on a's list. Tolerable defects stay local and intolerable ones go up, as b requires. Tolerability therefore marks where the group's autonomy ends. Statement a does not require every listed response to be available for every diagnosis. 'Review the agreement or the intent' can simply be another option alongside these, so nothing conflicts.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a lists the possible responses to a diagnosis: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Statement b lists the figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness), each with an image and the slop it names. Neither says anything about the other's subject, so b does not add or remove a response to a diagnosis. Concrete example: in one methodology, b's table defines the figures and slop exactly as given. A verification of an artefact finds an element written in the wrong language (form slop) and a term used before its definition (order slop). The diagnosis records scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location. The working group then chooses one of a's five responses, for example 'correct'. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

The statements cover different things and can both hold. Statement a lists the permitted responses to a diagnosis: accept, accept with reservations, correct, escalate, or review the agreement or the intent. Statement b describes the comparison loop as a delegated task that has its own agreement, runs autonomously inside, and is validated by the user at the end. Concrete example: a working group delegates the comparison loop and first settles its agreement on communication. The loop runs autonomously. At the end the user validates the result. If that validation is a verification, its diagnosis is graded by scope, severity, urgency, tolerability and location, and the user responds with one of a's options, for example 'accept with reservations', or 'review the agreement' if the loop's own agreement caused the failure. Neither statement restricts what the other requires: b does not demand any response outside a's list, and a says nothing about delegation, autonomy or end-validation.

Example: a comparison loop is delegated as a task under its own agreement. Each defect it meets is measured against the agreed threshold. All of them prove tolerable, so the loop resolves them itself without referring any decision upward. That makes it autonomous inside, with that autonomy bounded by tolerability as (a) requires. No defect is intolerable, so (a)'s escalation condition never triggers. At the end the user validates the result, as (b) requires. Validating the finished result is not a mid-task referral of decisions, so it does not break the loop's internal autonomy. Every clause of both statements holds.

b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. Even if read as the claim that autonomy depends on verifiability, both can hold together, because tolerability is classified by measuring a defect against a threshold, which presupposes that the result can be verified. Example: a team's agreement sets a defect threshold of 5%. A subtask result with a measured defect of 3% is judged tolerable and resolved at its own level, while 8% is escalated one level up. A result that cannot be measured cannot be classified as tolerable, so it is also escalated. Then tolerability marks the boundary of autonomy, as a requires, and more verifiable results can be delegated further, as b's reading requires.

The two statements fit together. Statement a makes an aesthetic claim: impeccable work (zero slop) is beautiful, slop introduces ugliness, and it offers two images, a line breaking the metre and a forced puzzle piece. Statement b is a table assigning those same two images to the same figures: the broken-metre line to form and the forced piece to fit. It then adds five more figures, each with its own image and examples of slop. This added detail does not conflict with a. Concrete example: a specification whose elements are all in the group's shared language, all traceable to the intent, with no contradictions, no repetition, every term defined before use, no ambiguous sentences, and every claim backed by evidence. It has zero slop, so it is impeccable and beautiful (a). Adding one element in the wrong language would be form slop under b, matching a's broken-metre image, and would introduce ugliness under a. Adding an element that contradicts another would be fit slop, matching a's forced-piece image. Every clause of both statements holds.

Example: an artefact made only of a heading 'Rules' and an element (id R1, kind rule, text 'Use UTC timestamps'), with no stray text. If 'any other text' means text outside headings and elements, it has zero slop, so it is impeccable and beautiful, as a says. Suppose stray prose is added between elements. That is slop of form under b, like a line breaking a poem's metre, and it introduces ugliness under a. Even on the stricter reading, where every non-heading text (including element text) counts as slop, a still holds: such artefacts simply carry slop and ugliness. a never requires any artefact to be impeccable. Neither reading creates a conflict.

Example: two documents checked against figures F1 (line breaks the metre) and F2 (piece forced into the wrong place). In document D1, no element breaks any figure. Its slop sum is 0, so it is impeccable under b, and we take it to be beautiful, satisfying a. In document D2, element e1 is a line that breaks the metre and is also forced into the wrong place, so it counts once in F1 and once in F2. Its unweighted slop is 2, so it is not impeccable, and its violations introduce ugliness, satisfying a's images. Statement a gives aesthetic judgements: impeccable means beautiful, and slop introduces ugliness. Statement b gives a counting rule: unweighted sum, counted per figure broken, impeccable if and only if the sum is zero. Both match the definition of impeccable as zero slop, and neither requires anything the other rules out.

The statements address different matters and fit together. Statement a describes how slop relates to beauty and ugliness. Statement b says the statistical verifier, like any candidate, is tested against a corpus whose slop is known. Example: a corpus holds two poems. One is impeccable (zero slop) and therefore beautiful. The other has one line that breaks the metre, a slop that makes it ugly. The verifier sends its fixed decision question N times to fixed decision models, and its judgement is checked against this known slop, just as a candidate would be checked against a corpus. Every clause of both statements holds.

Both statements name the same seven figures: form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. Statement b adds no figure and leaves none out, so a's exhaustive list holds. Its added images and slop examples are extra detail, and each matches the definitions: a wrong-language element breaks an established pattern (form); a contradicting or untraceable element is fit; saying the same thing twice is a removable element (economy); an undefined term is completeness; use before definition is order; two meanings or readings is sharpness; a claim of verification without evidence is truthfulness. Example: a methodology whose figure set is exactly these seven, each illustrated by the image and slop instances in b's table, satisfies every clause of both.

Example: the seven figures are exactly form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness, as a lists. A document artefact has the heading 'Rules', which is a label and is not measured. It also has element E1 (kind: rule, text: 'Each term is defined before use'). There is no other text, so b's structure holds, and its clause that any other text is slop of form is satisfied without exception. The two statements also fit together: b classifies stray text under form, and form is one of the figures a lists. a only enumerates the figures and makes no claim about artefact structure, so nothing conflicts.

Statement a names seven figures: form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness and truthfulness. Statement b's table has rows for exactly the same seven figures, with no extras and none missing, and gives the violations counted for each. Example satisfying both: a methodology whose only figures are these seven, each counted as b specifies. For instance, form counts malformed headers, duplicate identifiers and the other listed cases; fit counts untraceable elements and each minimal unsatisfiable subset; economy counts the size of Σ' minus the smallest equivalent subset; and so on through truthfulness, which counts claims without evidence. The violation details in b are added detail, not a conflict with a's list.

Statement a lists seven figures. Statement b sets an unweighted counting rule over those figures, so the two fit together. Example: a document has element E1 that uses an undefined term (completeness) and is ambiguous (sharpness). E1 counts once in each figure, so the document's slop is 2 and it is not impeccable. A second document breaks none of the seven figures, so its slop sum is 0 and it is impeccable. This matches b's 'if and only if' and the definition of impeccable as zero slop. Using 'slop' both for a single violation and for the total count is a loose use of the word, not a conflict.

The statements address different matters and fit together. a lists seven figures (form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness, truthfulness). b defines a candidate's error and when it passes. Concrete example: there is one corpus containing one artefact. Its true violations are {(Order, element e1, 'term X used before its definition'), (Truthfulness, element e2, 'claim Y without evidence')}, and every figure involved is one of a's seven. A candidate detects exactly these two triples on both of two runs. The symmetric difference is empty, so the error is 0 on every corpus (there is only one), and the output is identical across the two runs. The candidate therefore passes. A second candidate that misses one triple has error 1 and fails, which is consistent with b's 'only'. Nothing in a limits how errors are counted, and nothing in b limits which figures exist.

Statement a lists, for each figure, some kinds of slop. Under form it lists 'an element in the wrong language'. Statement b says an artefact consists of headings and elements, and that any other text is slop of form. That adds one more case of form slop. Form is defined as breaking a pattern the work has established, and b's heading-and-element structure is such a pattern, so stray text fits the definition. Nothing in a says its list is exhaustive, and silence is not a prohibition. Concrete example: a document has the heading 'Rules' and one element E1 of kind rule. E1 is written in the group's shared language. Every term in it is defined before it is used, it has a single reading, it derives from the intent and contradicts nothing, and any claim in it has evidence. There is no text other than the heading and E1. Every clause of both statements holds: b's structure is met, and a's classifications stand, with this artefact simply showing none of the listed slop.

The two statements cover different things and do not conflict. Statement a lists the kinds of defect (figures) and what counts as a violation of each. Statement b says how an element is written. Example artefact: the header line '[E1] {kind: claim; evidence: test log T7}' is followed by the text 'The parser rejects empty input.' That text runs until the next header line, '[E2] {kind: term}'. This matches b: the identifier is in square brackets, the metadata is in braces with key-value pairs separated by semicolons, and the text ends at the next header. It also fits the definition of an element, since it has an identifier, a kind (given in the metadata) and a text. Statement a's table can hold over this same artefact unchanged. For example, E1 with no evidence would be a truthfulness slop, and a second element repeating E1 would be an economy slop. Nothing in a governs the header syntax, and nothing in b redefines or forbids any of the figures.

The two statements cover different things and can both hold. Statement a is a table that maps each figure to the slop it names. Statement b is a schema of metadata keys. Example artefact: element D1 has kind definition, defines "claim", variants "claims", status proposal. Element C1 has kind claim, derives D1 and INTENT, evidence "test log 2024-05", status proposal. Element R1 has kind rule, derives AGREEMENT, status proposal. This follows every key in b: defines and variants appear only in a definition, derives appears on every non-definition, evidence appears only in a claim, and status is proposal. The figures and slop listed in a remain a valid classification of defects for this artefact. Where the two touch, they agree: b's evidence key for claims supports the truthfulness slop (a claim of verification without evidence), and b's derives key supports the fit slop (an element not traceable to the intent). Neither statement forbids anything the other requires.

Statement a is a rubric that classifies kinds of slop under seven figures. Statement b is a marking convention: each use of a term goes in double square brackets, using a variant its definition declares, and unmarked text is ordinary vocabulary. Neither sets a requirement the other forbids. Concrete example: a work writes '[[Claim]]' and '[[Evidence]]' in brackets wherever it uses those terms, defines each term before using it, and is checked against a's table. Under that table, an unsupported [[Claim]] counts as truthfulness slop and an undefined bracketed term counts as completeness slop. Both statements hold. Even if b is applied to a's own unbracketed words ('element', 'term', 'claim'), b's second sentence classes them as ordinary vocabulary rather than breaking the rule. So no clause of either statement is violated.

Example: the glossary holds the supplied definitions in the listed order. Each one uses only terms defined earlier and never its own term. For instance, 'Slop' uses 'figure', which is defined before it, and 'Truthfulness' uses 'claim' and 'evidence', both defined before it. The table in (a) sits in another artefact. It does not define its row labels; it only pairs each figure with an image and with examples of slop in this work. So no definition lives outside the glossary, and every clause of (b) holds alongside (a). (b) constrains only definitions, not where terms are used, so the table may freely use 'term', 'element' and 'intent'.

The answer depends on whether b's table is the complete list of violations. 'Slop' is defined as a violation of a figure, so every slop item in a must count as a violation. Reading 1 (b exhaustive, a illustrative): a counts 'a sentence with two readings' as sharpness slop. b counts sharpness only as multiply-defined terms, variants declared by more than one term, and vague-list words. An ambiguous sentence with none of these, such as a scope ambiguity with no listed vague word, would be slop under a but not a violation under b. Likewise, 'an element in the wrong language' would be form slop under a, but b only catches three or more Spanish stopwords in one element; foreign-language text with fewer such words is missed. These requirements cannot both hold, so the pair contradicts. Reading 2 (b is a partial operational count): b may detect only some slop, or add checks a omits, such as malformed headers, any claim without evidence, and self-referential definitions. Extra detail is not a contradiction, and the remaining rows (completeness, order, economy, fit, truthfulness) line up or are narrower versions of each other. Under this reading the pair is compatible. Neither text settles whether b is exhaustive.

Statement a lists the figures and what counts as slop for each. Statement b only says how to count: each element counts in every figure it breaks, totals are unweighted, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when the total is zero. Nothing in a sets weights or limits an element to one figure, so b just adds detail. Example: document D has element E1, a term used without a definition (one completeness slop), and element E2, a sentence that has two readings and also uses a word outside the shared language (one sharpness slop plus one form slop, since E2 counts in both figures). D's slop is 1+1+1=3, so D is not impeccable. A second document D' with no violations in any of a's seven figures has slop 0 and is impeccable. Both examples satisfy every clause of a, b and the definitions (Slop = a violation of a figure; Impeccable = zero slop).

Statement a only catalogues the figures and their slop. Fit covers 'an element that contradicts another' and economy covers 'the same thing said twice'. Statement b proposes how two of those slops are counted: formalise elements as logical formulas, count contradictions as minimal unsatisfiable subsets, and treat an element as redundant when the rest entails it. A concrete example satisfying both: a methodology keeps a's seven-figure table unchanged. It writes each element as an axiom in a decidable description logic. A reasoner finds the minimal unsatisfiable subsets, and each one is counted as fit slop. Each element entailed by the remaining elements is counted as economy slop; a restated element is one such case. The contradiction and redundancy judgements are made once, when the elements are formalised, and recorded, rather than repeated at each point-in-time verification. Nothing in a fixes when or how its slops are judged, and b says nothing about the other figures. b's redundancy test is broader than 'said twice', but that adds detail rather than conflicting. The definition of figure as 'counted by a formula' fits b's approach.

Statement a is a taxonomy: it says that, under the economy figure, 'the same thing said twice' counts as slop. Statement b is a procedure for judging redundancy until a logic is chosen. A work can hold both. Example: a work uses a's table. Elements E1 and E2 both use the term 'Slop', so they are compared. A versioned yes/no question with typed yes/no criteria goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. The model whose output repeats exactly runs once and the other runs three times. Element pairs that share no term are not compared. Nothing in a says how redundancy must be detected, or that every pair of elements must be checked. So b's narrower comparison scope only limits what this procedure examines; it does not deny a's definition. The varying run counts also fit the definition of a statistical verifier as a fixed question sent N times to fixed decision models.

The two statements cover different matters. Statement a lists the figures and the slop that counts under each. Statement b sets the procedure for deciding whether an element is a defect. Neither requires anything the other forbids. Example: an element written in the wrong language (form slop) is checked by a panel of two models. Every run returns a probability p, each run is decided yes under SLP.24, no request fails the schema and no run is missing. Under statement b the element is therefore decided a defect, which fits statement a's account of it as form slop. The reference SLP.24 is not defined in this pair, but it does not create a conflict.

Statement a is a table that classifies kinds of defect (slop) under each figure. Under fit, one listed slop is 'an element that contradicts another'. Statement b describes how contradiction is judged until a logic is chosen. It does not redefine any figure or slop that a lists. Example satisfying both: a methodology adopts a's table as its figures. To detect the fit slop 'an element that contradicts another', it sends each pair of elements that share a term, alone with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The template is calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash. A 'contradiction' reply naming the incompatible requirements is counted as a fit slop. A 'compatible' reply with a satisfying example is not. A 'refer' reply is escalated to the user. A schema failure or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete and counts as no decision. This is consistent with a's truthfulness row, since no verification is claimed without evidence. Every clause of both statements holds in this setup.

Statement a only classifies kinds of defect (figures) and gives examples of slop. It does not require any artefact to be free of them, and it imposes no rule on how judgements are stored or reused. Statement b describes a caching mechanism: each judgement is recorded with its input hash, template hash, models, N and k, and is re-run only when a hash changes. Concrete example: a methodology defines the seven figures as in a's table. Its tool stores each judgement, e.g. a sharpness judgement of element E1, alongside hash(E1 text), hash(template), the model list, N=5 and k=3. The next verification finds both hashes unchanged and reuses the recorded result. If E1 is later edited, its hash changes and E1 is judged again. Every clause of both statements holds. Reusing a recorded judgement is not 'a claim of verification without evidence': the stored record, keyed by hashes, is the evidence. That b leaves N and k undefined would at most be a completeness defect in the wording, not a logical conflict with a.

Statement a only lists the figures and what counts as slop for each, such as a term used before its definition or a claim of verification without evidence. Statement b only says the statistical verifier is tested against a corpus with known slop, as candidates are. Example: a methodology adopts a's table. It builds a corpus of artefacts seeded with known slop, for instance one artefact with a term used and not defined and another with a sentence that has two readings. It sends its fixed decision question N times to fixed decision models over that corpus to see whether the verifier's probabilities detect the known slop, and evaluates candidates against a corpus the same way. Every row of a and the requirement in b are met, and nothing in a forbids evaluating the verifier.

Statement a lists seven figures and what counts as slop (a violation of a figure) under each, for example a term used before its definition under order. Statement b defines how a candidate is scored against such violations: error is the size of the symmetric difference between the detected and true violation sets, and passing requires zero error on every corpus plus identical output on two runs. One describes the violation kinds; the other describes the scoring, and nothing in either clashes with the other. Concrete example: a corpus with one artefact whose element E2 uses the term 'Intent' before element E5 defines it. The true set is {(order, E2, 'Intent' before definition)}. A deterministic candidate outputs exactly that set on both runs. Its error is 0 and the two outputs are identical, so it passes. The violation is an order slop exactly as a describes it, so every clause of both statements holds.

Example artefact: a heading line '# Rules', then the header line '[R1] {kind: rule; owner: ana}', then the text 'Every claim cites a source.', then the next heading '# Results'. The artefact consists only of headings and elements, so a is met. The heading is a label and is not measured. No text lies outside a heading or an element, so nothing is slop of form. The element meets b: its header line gives the identifier in square brackets, then metadata in braces as key-value pairs separated by semicolons, with the kind among them. Its text runs to the next heading. b only adds detail about how an element is laid out. Under a's natural reading, 'any other text' means text that is neither heading nor element. This example avoids such text.

Example artefact: one heading 'Rules' and one element R1 with metadata kind: rule, derives: INTENT, status: proposal, and the text 'Each element has an identifier.' It has no defines, variants or evidence keys, which b allows only in definitions or claims. Derives is present because the element is not a definition, and status is proposal because it is not yet validated, so every clause of b holds. The metadata is part of the element: an element by definition has an identifier, a kind and a text, and 'kind' is one of b's keys. So the artefact contains only headings and elements, there is no other text, and nothing is slop of form under a.

The answer depends on what b's 'malformed header' means. Shared ground: a calls any text outside headings and elements slop of form, and b's form row lists 'text outside elements and headings', so the two agree there. Reading 1: 'header' means an element's header (its identifier, kind and keys). This fits the neighbouring items in b (duplicate identifier, invalid kind, missing required key). Under this reading b never measures headings. The pair is compatible, for example with an artefact made of well-formed headings and fully traced, defined, evidenced elements that triggers no violation. Reading 2: 'header' means a heading. Then b counts a malformed heading as a form violation, and that measures headings, which a says are 'not measured'. A rule that counts them conflicts with a rule that exempts them, so the pair contradicts. A similar question arises in b's sharpness row: it counts each occurrence of a vague-word entry with no stated exclusion for headings. If that scan includes heading text, it also measures headings.

Example: an artefact has the heading 'Scope' and one element (id E1, kind rule, text 'Use UTC timestamps'). It contains no other text, and E1 breaks no figure. Statement a holds: the artefact is made only of headings and elements, the heading is not measured, and there is no stray text to count as slop of form. Statement b holds: each figure's violations are counted without weights, the sum is 0, and the artefact is impeccable. The two statements fit together. A adds one source of form slop (stray text), and b says how all slop is summed and when an artefact is impeccable. Under a stricter reading of 'any other text', where even element text counts as form slop, the same artefact has slop 1 and is not impeccable. That still violates neither statement, because b never requires any artefact to be impeccable.

Take an artefact with one heading, 'Axioms', and three elements, each with an identifier, kind 'axiom' and a formula as its text, in ALC (a decidable description logic): E1 'A ⊑ B', E2 'B ⊑ C', E3 'A ⊑ C'. There is no other text, so statement a holds: the heading is an unmeasured label and the elements are the only remaining text. Statement b holds too: E3 is redundant because E1 and E2 entail it, and the set has no minimal unsatisfiable subset, so the counts are 0 contradictions and 1 redundancy. These judgements are made once when the elements are formalised and are recorded, for example as elements of a separate record artefact, so they add no stray text to this one. Writing element texts as formulas does not create text outside headings and elements.

Example: no logic has been chosen. The artefact is a document with one heading, 'Rules', which is a label and is not measured. It has three elements and no other text, so there is no slop of form. E1 (kind: rule, text: 'A term names a concept'). E2 (kind: rule, text: 'Each term names one concept'). E3 (kind: rule, text: 'Code is checked'). E1 and E2 share the term 'term', so they are compared. E3 shares no term with them and is not compared. The comparison uses versioned question v1: 'Is E2 redundant given E1?' It has typed criteria for yes (same claim, same scope) and for no (adds or changes a claim). The question is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned models google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Gemini's output repeats exactly, so it is run once. The Perplexity model's output varies, so it is run three times. This fits the definition of a fixed question sent to fixed models, if N is read as set per model. Statement a governs what an artefact contains and what counts as slop of form. Statement b governs how redundancy between elements is judged. No clause of either is violated.

Example: an artefact has one heading, 'Scope', and one element E1 (identifier E1, kind 'claim', text 'The rule applies to all inputs'). There is no other text, so nothing counts as slop of form. The heading is a label and is not measured. E1 is verified by a panel of two models with two runs each. Every request passes the schema, so there are no failures and no missing runs. Each run returns a probability p and is decided under SLP.24. Whatever SLP.24 specifies, each run gets a decision. If all four runs are decided yes, E1 is a defect. If all are no, E1 is not a defect. Any mix escalates E1 to the user. Every clause of both statements holds. Statement a governs what the artefact is made of and what is measured. Statement b governs how measured elements are decided. They do not conflict.

a constrains how an artefact is composed: only headings and elements, with any other text counting as slop of form. b describes how contradiction between pairs of elements is judged. b never requires an artefact to contain text that is neither a heading nor an element. Concrete example: a methodology document whose content is the heading 'Contradiction' followed by one element (with an identifier, kind 'rule' and a text) stating b's procedure. The glossary is a separate artefact made of headings and one element per term definition. Two elements sharing the term 'Verification' are sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using the template identified by its SHA-256 hash, together with the definitions of the terms either element uses. The model replies 'compatible' with a satisfying example. A different pair gets 'refer', which is escalated to the user. A schema-failing reply leaves that verification incomplete and is not counted as a decision. Every artefact contains only headings and elements, so a holds, and every clause of b holds.

The two statements govern different things: (a) says what an artefact is made of and that stray text counts as slop of form; (b) says the verifier is tested on a corpus with known slop. Example: a corpus contains document D1. D1 has the heading 'Rules', which is not measured, and element R1 (identifier R1, kind rule, text 'Each rule names one figure'). D1 also has a stray sentence that sits outside any heading or element. Under (a) that sentence is slop of form, and the corpus marks it as known slop. The statistical verifier is a fixed question ('Does this text break the established pattern?') sent N=5 times to fixed models. It is scored against the known slop in this corpus in the same way as any candidate, which satisfies (b). Nothing in (a) forbids testing the verifier, and nothing in (b) changes how artefacts are made up.

Example: the only corpus holds one artefact, made of the heading 'Rules' and element E1 (kind 'rule', text 'Keep lists short'). No other text is present. Statement a says the heading is an unmeasured label. If 'any other text' means text outside headings and elements, there are no violations. The candidate outputs the empty set on both runs, so the symmetric difference is 0 and the output is identical. If it means all non-heading text, the true set is {(form, E1, 'non-heading text')}. The candidate outputs exactly that triple on both runs, again giving error 0 and identical output. Either way every clause of a and b holds. Statement b only defines how a candidate is scored and passed. Nothing in it conflicts with a's account of how an artefact is built or which text counts as slop of form.

Statement a sets the syntax of the header line. Statement b lists which metadata keys may appear and what values they take. They govern different aspects and do not conflict. A concrete example: the header line `[C1] {kind=claim; derives=INTENT; evidence=user survey 2023; status=proposal}` is followed by the text 'Most users prefer dark mode.', which runs until the next header line `[D1] {kind=definition; defines=Mode; variants=theme; status=proposal}`. C1 satisfies a: identifier in square brackets, then metadata in braces as semicolon-separated key-value pairs, then text up to the next header. C1 also satisfies b: kind is claim, derives is present because C1 is not a definition, evidence appears only in a claim, and status is proposal because it is not yet validated. D1 likewise satisfies both: defines and variants appear in a definition, and derives may be omitted there.

Both can hold in one methodology. (a) sets the element syntax. (b) only defines how each figure counts violations, and nothing in it bans what (a) requires. Several entries in (b) build on (a): 'a malformed header' assumes a header pattern such as the one (a) gives, and 'duplicate identifier', 'invalid kind' and 'missing required key' fit the bracketed identifier and the braced key-value metadata. 'Text outside elements and headings' fits (a)'s rule that an element's text runs to the next header line or heading. Concrete example: an artefact with the heading '# Rules', then '[R1] {kind: rule; source: INTENT}' followed by 'Each request is logged.', then '[D1] {kind: definition; term: request}' followed by 'A message sent by a client.' Every element starts with a header line in (a)'s format, and each text ends at the next header. Read against (b)'s figures: R1 traces to INTENT and D1 is traceable because R1 uses its term, so fit counts nothing. There are no claims, so truthfulness counts nothing. There are no duplicate identifiers or definitions and no vague words. The only possible count is order, because R1 uses 'request' before D1 defines it, and that is a violation count, not a conflict between the statements. Placing D1 first gives a zero-violation instance. The figure definitions agree with (b)'s table.

Statement a sets the syntax of an element: a bracketed identifier, braced key-value metadata separated by semicolons, and text running to the next header or heading. Statement b sets how slop is counted: an element counts once in every figure it breaks, the artefact's slop is the unweighted sum over all figures, and the artefact is impeccable if and only if that sum is zero. The two concern different things and do not conflict. Example: a document holds '[E1] {kind: rule; owner: Ann}' followed by text, then '[E2] {kind: note; owner: Bo}' followed by text that ends at a heading. Two figures are defined. E1 breaks both figures and counts in each; E2 breaks neither. Slop = 1 + 1 = 2, so the document is not impeccable. If E1 is fixed, the sum is 0 and the document is impeccable. Every clause of both statements holds.

Statement a sets the surface syntax of an element: a bracketed identifier, brace-delimited metadata as semicolon-separated key-value pairs, and text running to the next header or heading. Statement b says what the element's content should be when written logically: a formula in a decidable logic such as a description logic. Nothing in either requires the other to fail, because the text of an a-style element can itself be a description-logic axiom. Concrete example: header '[E1]{kind: axiom; author: Ana}' with text 'Dog ⊑ Animal'; header '[E2]{kind: axiom; author: Ben}' with text 'Dog ⊑ ¬Animal'; header '[E3]{kind: axiom; author: Ana}' with text 'Dog ⊓ Cat ⊑ Animal'. Each text runs to the next header, satisfying a. Each element has an identifier, a kind (in the metadata) and a text, matching the definition of Element. Written in the decidable logic ALC, the set lets you count contradictions: with Dog required to be satisfiable (if the dictionary is allowed to be empty, E1 and E2 alone are consistent), {E1, E2} is a minimal unsatisfiable subset. It also lets you count redundancy: E3 follows from E1, so E1 and E2 together entail it. These judgements are made once when the elements are formalised and recorded, for example as metadata entries such as 'conflicts: E2' or 'redundant: true', which a's metadata format accommodates. All clauses of both statements hold together.

The two statements cover separate matters: (a) the format of an element, and (b) how redundancy between elements is judged. A single example satisfies both. Element E1 begins with the header line `[E1]{kind: rule; version: 1}`, and its text 'Each Term names a concept.' runs to the next header. Element E2 begins with `[E2]{kind: rule}`, and its text 'A Term is a named concept.' runs to the heading '## Notes'. This fits the definition of an element: E1 and E2 are identifiers, the kind is in the metadata, and each has a text. No logic has been chosen yet, so redundancy is judged by a statistical verifier. That verifier is question v1, 'Is E2 redundant given E1?', with typed criteria for yes and for no. It is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned models google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Suppose gemini's output repeats exactly, so it runs once, while pplx's does not, so it runs three times. That still fits the definition's 'sent N times', with N set per model. E1 and E2 share the term 'Term', so they are compared. An element E3 that shares no term with either is never compared. Every clause of both statements holds in this example.

Statement a only describes how an element is laid out: a header line, then text. Statement b only describes how runs are decided and aggregated. Neither constrains the other. Example: an artefact contains the line '[E1] {kind: requirement; owner: ana}' followed by 'The system shall log every login.', and the next line is '[E2] {...}'. So E1's text runs exactly to the next header. Two panel models each make one schema-valid request about E1, giving two runs. Each run returns a probability, e.g. p=0.9 and p=0.85. No request fails the schema, so there are no failures. No run is missing, so the verification is complete. Whatever SLP.24 decides for these values, E1 receives exactly one outcome: defect if both runs are yes, no defect if both are no, escalated to the user otherwise. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things: (a) sets the textual format of an element, and (b) sets how contradiction between elements is judged before a logic is chosen. Neither requirement limits the other. Example: an artefact contains element lines such as '[E1] {kind: rule; status: active}', each followed by text running to the next header or heading. No logic has been chosen yet. Each pair of elements that share a term is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The request uses the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash, and includes the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses. Each reply is contradiction (naming the conflicting requirements), compatible (with a satisfying example) or refer. Refers are escalated to the user. A reply that fails the schema, or a transport failure, leaves the verification incomplete and counts as no decision. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements cover different things. (a) defines how an element is written; (b) defines a candidate's error and a necessary condition for passing. Neither constrains the other. Example: an artefact contains the header line '[E1] {kind=note; owner=x}' followed by text that runs to the next header line '[E2] {kind=rule; owner=y}', then E2's text up to a heading. This satisfies (a): the identifier is in brackets, the metadata is key-value pairs in braces separated by semicolons, and each element's text ends at the next header or heading. The test uses a single corpus containing this artefact. Its true violation set is {(figure F1, element E1, detail 'missing owner tag')}. A candidate detects exactly that set, so the symmetric difference is empty and the error is 0 on every corpus. It produces identical output on two runs. It therefore meets (b)'s requirement for passing. 'Passes only with' is a necessary condition, and nothing here violates it.

Statement a defines the metadata schema. Statement b lists what counts as a violation of each figure. One artefact can satisfy both with zero violations. Example: element D1 has kind definition, defines 'foo', no variants, status proposal, no derives (allowed for a definition), and its text does not use 'foo'. Element R1 has kind rule, derives INTENT, status proposal, and uses the marked term 'foo' after D1. Element C1 has kind claim, derives R1, evidence 'measurement log', status proposal. All text sits inside elements or headings, with no stopword or vague-word hits. This triggers no form, fit, economy, completeness, order, sharpness or truthfulness violations. The schema and the violations agree: 'missing required key' matches derives being required outside definitions, the fit rule matches the derives targets INTENT and AGREEMENT, and truthfulness counting a claim without evidence fits evidence being allowed only in claims. Statement a never makes evidence mandatory, so a claim lacking it is simply a counted defect, not a conflict.

The two statements cover different matters. Statement a sets which metadata keys an element carries. Statement b sets how violations are counted and when an artefact is impeccable. Nothing in either constrains the other. Example: an artefact with one element E1 whose metadata is kind: claim, derives: [INTENT], evidence: 'measurement log', status: proposal. It has no defines or variants because it is not a definition, and derives is present because it is not a definition. This satisfies a. Under b, suppose E1 breaks figures F1 and F2. It counts in each, so with no weights the slop is 2 and the artefact is not impeccable. Remove those defects and the sum is 0, making it impeccable. Both statements hold throughout.

The two statements cover different things. (a) defines a metadata schema for elements; (b) describes writing element texts as logical formulas and judging contradiction and redundancy there. Nothing in (a) forbids formalised texts, and nothing in (b) restricts metadata keys. Example: element D1 has kind=definition, defines='Cat', variants=['Feline'], status=proposal, and its text is recorded as the ALC axiom Cat ≡ Feline ⊓ Animal. Element C1 has kind=claim, derives=['D1','INTENT'], evidence='field survey', status=proposal, and its text is the ALC axiom Cat ⊑ ∃eats.Fish. Element R1 has kind=rule, derives=['AGREEMENT'], status=proposal, and its text is Animal ⊑ ¬Plant. ALC is a decidable description logic, so a reasoner can count minimal unsatisfiable subsets (none here) and check whether any element is entailed by the rest (none here). That judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded. Each element still carries status=proposal until validated, which (b) does not forbid. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements govern different things. a sets the metadata keys an element may carry. b sets how redundancy is judged before a logic is chosen. Neither restricts the other, and run counts that differ per model still fit 'sent N times' in the definition. Example: element D1 has kind=definition, defines=['statistical verifier'], variants=['verifier'], status=proposal and no derives. Element C1 has kind=claim, derives=['D1'], evidence='benchmark log', status=proposal. Element R1 has kind=rule, derives=['INTENT'], status=proposal. Until a logic is chosen, redundancy is checked with question v1, which is yes/no and has typed yes and no criteria. It goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned panel google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Only D1 and C1 share a term ('statistical verifier'), so only that pair is compared. Gemini's output repeats exactly, so it is run once. Pplx is run three times. Every clause of both statements holds.

The two statements govern different things. Statement a sets the metadata keys an element may carry. Statement b sets how a verification's runs are aggregated into a decision. Nothing in either constrains the other. Concrete example: element E7 has kind claim, derives [INTENT], evidence "vendor datasheet, section 3" and status proposal. It has no defines or variants, as required outside a definition. A verification checks E7 with a panel of two models, each run once. Each run returns a probability p, for example 0.95 and 0.97, and each is decided yes under SLP.24, assuming those values fall on the yes side of its rule. Every run of every panel model is decided yes, so E7 is decided as a defect. No request fails the schema and no run is missing, so the verification is complete. Every clause of a and b holds.

The two statements cover different matters, so both can hold. Statement a sets the metadata keys an element may carry. Statement b sets how contradiction between elements is judged before a logic is chosen. Example: the artefact has two elements, R1 and C1, that share a term. R1 has kind rule, derives INTENT, status proposal, and no defines, variants or evidence. C1 has kind claim, derives R1, evidence with its supporting source, and status proposal. During verification, R1 and C1 are sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt identified by its SHA-256 hash, together with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses. The model replies 'compatible' with an example satisfying both, and that counts as a decision. If another pair returns 'refer', it is escalated to the user. If a reply fails the schema or transport fails, the verification is left incomplete and no decision is counted. Every clause of a (allowed kinds, where defines, variants and evidence may appear, derives required outside definitions, status proposal until validated) and of b (model, temperature, template, one pair per request, glossary context, the three reply types, escalation, incomplete-verification handling) is satisfied. The reply 'evidence' in b is the model's output, not the element metadata key 'evidence', so the two do not clash.

The statements cover different things. Statement a sets out the metadata schema for elements. Statement b defines a candidate's error and when it passes. Neither constrains the other. Example: corpus C1 contains one artefact. Its element E1 has kind=claim, derives=[INTENT], evidence='benchmark log' and status=proposal. That uses defines/variants only in definitions, evidence only in a claim, and derives in a non-definition, so it satisfies a. Its element E2 has kind=definition, defines='Figure' and variants=['defect kind'], with no derives and no evidence, also satisfying a. Candidate K, run on C1, detects {(F1, E1, 'evidence unsupported')}. The true violation set is the same, so the symmetric difference is empty and the error is 0. C1 is the only corpus, so K has zero error on every corpus. A second run gives identical output, so K passes and b holds.

A glossary in this order satisfies both statements. Entry 1 has the headword Term, declared variants 'term' and 'terms', and the definition 'A word or phrase that names a concept of this methodology.' It uses no terms, and 'methodology' is unmarked ordinary vocabulary. Entry 2 has the headword Glossary, declared variant 'glossary', and the definition 'The artefact that holds the definition of every [[term]].' It uses only Term, which was defined before it, marked in a declared variant, and it never uses its own term. All definitions are in the glossary, and every term use elsewhere is bracketed. The example assumes the headword and the variant declarations are part of the entry's structure, not uses of the term inside its own definition. Statement b restricts which terms a definition uses, and statement a governs how term uses are written. The two do not conflict.

Statement a is a marking convention: every use of a term goes in double square brackets, in one of the variants its definition declares, and unmarked text is ordinary vocabulary. Statement b lists counted violations. One of them, 'an unmarked occurrence of a declared variant', enforces a's convention rather than opposing it. b's completeness row ('a marked term that no definition declares') fits a's requirement that marks use declared variants. Concrete example: an artefact with an INTENT element whose text reads 'Each [[claim]] needs [[evidence]]'. The definitions of Claim and Evidence declare those variants, define themselves without using their own term, and appear before the element. No declared variant appears unmarked, and the text has no stopwords or vague words. Every term use is marked in a declared variant, so a holds. b's rules apply and count zero violations, so b holds as well. Possible tension: a's second sentence treats unmarked text as ordinary vocabulary, while b still flags unmarked occurrences of declared-variant words. Read as a permission to use those words unmarked, this would conflict with b. But a only classifies such text and does not permit it. The example avoids unmarked variants entirely, so both statements are satisfied either way.

Concrete example: an artefact writes every term use in double square brackets, using a variant its definition declares, for example [[Element]]. Unmarked words are ordinary vocabulary. Two elements, E1 and E2, both contain [[Term X]], so they share a term and are compared. E3 shares no term with them and is not compared. No logic has been chosen yet, so their redundancy is judged by a versioned yes/no decision question with typed yes and no criteria. It is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to google/gemini-decision-1, which is run once because its output repeats exactly, and to perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2, which is run three times. This fits the definition of a statistical verifier: a fixed question sent N times to fixed models, where N is 1 or 3 per model. Statement a governs how terms are marked; statement b governs how redundancy is judged and which elements are compared. Marking actually makes 'share a term' checkable. Possible objection: b itself uses words like 'statistical verifier', 'element' and 'term' without brackets. Under a, unmarked text simply counts as ordinary vocabulary, so this changes how those words are read but creates no conflict.

Example: a methodology's artefacts write every glossary term in double square brackets, such as [[Element]] or [[Term]], using a variant the definition declares. Unmarked words count as ordinary vocabulary. No logic has been chosen yet. Each pair of elements that share a marked term is sent alone, with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt is the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash. Replies are contradiction (naming the requirements that cannot hold together), compatible (with an example) or refer, and each refer is escalated to the user. A schema failure or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete and counts as no decision. Statement a governs how terms are marked in text. Statement b governs how contradiction is judged and how replies are handled. Neither forbids or requires anything the other affects. b's own wording leaves words like 'term' and 'element' unbracketed. Under a, those words are simply ordinary vocabulary, which may be a formalisation lapse in b's text but does not stop both statements from holding at once.

Example: a glossary holds all definitions in an order where each uses only earlier terms and never its own. For instance, Artefact, then Element (uses 'artefact'), then Term, Glossary, Figure, Form, through Claim, Evidence (uses 'claim') and Truthfulness (uses 'claim' and 'evidence'). A separate rules document holds b's table. The table lists violations and how each figure is counted; it does not place definitions outside the glossary. Under this example the glossary scores zero on b's 'a definition that uses its own term' and zero 'order' pairs, so both statements hold. b only counts breaches of what a requires and adds checks a does not mention. That extra detail is not a contradiction.

The answer depends on how b's colon clause is read. If it is a definition, the pair contradicts; if it only describes the verifier configuration being used, a compatible case exists. (1) Definition reading: b says 'a statistical verifier: a versioned yes-or-no decision question with typed criteria…'. Read this way, b defines 'statistical verifier' in a rule, not in the glossary. That breaks a's requirement that definitions live only in the glossary. The glossary entry is also different: it speaks of a fixed question sent N times and says nothing of versioning or typed criteria. So b would give the term a second, out-of-glossary definition. (2) Configuration reading: the glossary keeps the only definition, and b just names the setup used until a logic is chosen. The glossary can then be ordered Term, Glossary, Element, Statistical verifier, with each entry using only earlier terms and never its own. b's extra detail is then additional detail, not a conflict. A smaller tension remains: the glossary's single 'sent N times' sits uneasily with b's per-model counts (one run for a model with exactly repeating output, three runs for the other). It fits only if N may vary per model.

Example: the glossary is the only place with definitions, and lists them in the order Term, Element, Glossary, Verification. Term uses no defined term. Element and Verification use 'artefact', which is undefined here and not one of the four terms. Glossary uses only Term, which comes before it. No definition uses its own term. Until a logic is chosen, each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone, with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0 using the hash-identified template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt. Each reply is contradiction (naming the clashing requirements), compatible (with an example) or refer. Refers go to the user, and schema or transport failures leave the verification incomplete without counting as a decision. b is a procedure, not a definition placed outside the glossary, and it draws its definitions from the glossary, so both statements hold.

The table in a defines what counts as a violation in each figure. b only adds how to combine them: each figure counts on its own with no deduplication across figures, totals are summed with no weights, and zero means impeccable. Nothing in b changes a's formulas. Example: an artefact with one element, E1, which is traceable to INTENT, uses no terms and is a claim without evidence, but whose header is malformed. E1 counts once in form and once in truthfulness. Fit, economy, completeness, order and sharpness are all 0. Slop is 1+1=2, so the artefact is not impeccable. If E1 had a well-formed header and cited evidence, every figure would be 0, slop would be 0, and the artefact would be impeccable. This matches both 'Impeccable: having zero slop' and b's 'if and only if'. Two points look like conflicts but are not. First, figures that count non-element items (economy's size difference, completeness's terms, order's pairs) still feed the same sum. b's sentence about elements does not say that only elements count. Second, the definition 'Slop: a violation of a figure' fits b's total if slop is read as the number of such violations.

The two fit together. Statement a's fit row counts each minimal unsatisfiable subset, which matches b's definition of a contradiction. Its economy row measures removable elements, which matches b's notion of redundancy. Nothing in a requires verification rather than formalisation to make the judgement, and nothing rules out a decidable description logic. Example: an artefact has three elements, each well-formed, with defined terms that are used after their definitions, no vague words, no claims, and each derived from INTENT. Written in the description logic ALC: E1 A ⊑ B, E2 B ⊑ C, E3 A ⊑ C. The logical judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded, then verification counts. There is no minimal unsatisfiable subset, so fit = 0. Σ' = {E1, E2, E3}, and its smallest equivalent subset is {E1, E2}, so economy = 1. By b's test, only E3 is entailed by the rest, so exactly one element is redundant. Both statements' clauses hold. Their counting methods can diverge elsewhere; for example, two mutually equivalent elements give 2 redundant elements by b's test but economy = 1. However, b never says economy must equal that count, so this is not a contradiction.

Statement a gives the economy formula: the size of Σ' minus the size of the smallest subset equivalent to Σ'. It never says how equivalence or redundancy is decided. Statement b fills that gap for the period before a logic is chosen: a statistical verifier makes the judgement. That matches the definition of a statistical verifier: a fixed question sent N times to fixed models. N can be 1 for a model whose output repeats exactly and 3 for any other model. Example satisfying every clause of both statements: an artefact has elements E1 and E2. Both use the term 'Claim', and E2 restates E1. Neither element is in any minimal unsatisfiable subset, so Σ' = {E1, E2}. No logic has been chosen. A versioned yes/no question with typed yes and no criteria is sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API. It goes once to google/gemini-decision-1, whose output repeats exactly, and three times to perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2, whose output varies. The panel judges E2 redundant given E1. The smallest equivalent subset is {E1}, so economy = 2 − 1 = 1. The only redundancy lies between elements that share a term, so b's comparison restriction does not change the count. Every row of a's table can still apply as written.

The two statements describe different things, so both can hold at once. Statement a is a table saying what counts as a violation for each figure. Statement b is a procedure for deciding whether an element is a defect from panel-model runs. Neither forbids what the other requires. Concrete example: an artefact has one element, a claim with evidence, that uses no undefined, vague or misordered terms and is well formed. It traces to INTENT, sits in no unsatisfiable subset, and its set is already minimal. Every figure in a therefore counts zero violations. The panel has one model, and each of its runs schema-valid requests and returns a probability p. SLP.24 is unspecified, so we posit a reading under which it maps that p to no. Every run of every panel model is then decided no, so the element is decided as no defect. No request fails the schema and no run is missing, so the verification is complete. Every clause of both statements is satisfied.

The two statements govern different things, so one scenario can satisfy both. A defines what counts as a violation for each figure. For fit, that includes each minimal unsatisfiable subset of elements. B says how contradiction is judged before a logic is chosen: pairwise, by the named model at temperature 0, with the hashed template, given the glossary definitions of terms either element uses. Concrete example: no logic has been chosen. An artefact has elements E1, E2 and E3. E1 and E2 share a term, and each is satisfiable alone. That pair is sent alone with its definitions, and the schema-valid reply is contradiction, naming the clashing requirements. Every other term-sharing pair gets compatible with an example. No reply is refer, and no schema or transport failure occurs, so the verification is complete. Fit counts {E1,E2} as one minimal unsatisfiable subset. Economy is then computed on Σ' = {E3}. The other figures are counted as A specifies. If a pair had returned refer, B would only add escalation to the user; A forbids nothing about that. B's pairwise judging may miss unsatisfiable subsets of three or more elements, but A does not say how such subsets are detected, so this is a possible gap in coverage, not a contradiction.

Statement a lists which violations count under each figure. Statement b defines a candidate's error as the size of the symmetric difference between the detected and true violation sets, and says a candidate passes only with zero error on every corpus and identical output on two runs. One works as the ground truth and the other as the scoring rule, so they can both hold. Concrete example: the only corpus is one artefact. Its first element is well-formed, has kind INTENT and makes no claim. Its second element is a well-formed claim derived from the first, with no evidence. It uses no marked terms, has no definitions, no vague words, no Spanish stopwords and no unsatisfiable subsets. Neither element can be removed without loss, so economy is 0. Under a, the true set is exactly one violation: (truthfulness, element 2, claim without evidence). A deterministic candidate outputs exactly that violation on both runs. Its error is 0 on the only corpus and its output is identical across runs, so it passes under b. Every clause of both statements is satisfied. Economy being a count and fit violations being element subsets might make the figure/element/detail identification harder in other corpora. That does not prevent this example.

Example: an artefact has elements e1 'A ⊑ B', e2 'B ⊑ C' and e3 'A ⊑ C'. They are formalised once in the decidable description logic ALC, and the translation is recorded. The figures are contradiction (counted as minimal unsatisfiable subsets) and redundancy (an element the rest entails). The set is satisfiable, so there are no minimal unsatisfiable subsets and no contradiction slop. e3 is entailed by {e1, e2}, so it is redundant. Neither e1 nor e2 is entailed by the others. Each figure an element breaks counts once, unweighted, giving slop = 0 + 1 = 1, so the artefact is not impeccable. If e3 is removed, the sum is 0 and the artefact is impeccable. a fixes how violations are summed; b fixes how two figures detect violations and where the judgement is made. Neither conflicts with the other.

Statement a sets the counting rule: violations are summed over all figures with no weights, and an artefact is impeccable only if the sum is zero. Statement b sets how redundancy, one possible figure, is detected before a logic is chosen. The two can hold together. Example: an artefact has elements E1, E2 and E3. E1 and E2 share the term 'Figure', so they are compared. The versioned yes/no redundancy question, with typed yes and no criteria, goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned panel. google/gemini-decision-1 gives non-repeating output, so it is run three times. perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2 repeats exactly, so it is run once. The panel judges the pair redundant, which is one redundancy violation. E3 shares no term with the others, so it is not compared for redundancy, and it happens to be non-redundant. E3 breaks one other figure once. E1, E2 and E3 each count in every figure they break. Slop = 1 + 1 = 2, unweighted, so the artefact is not impeccable. The differing run counts per model fit the definition's 'sent N times', and the term-sharing restriction only limits which pairs the verifier compares. It does not conflict with pure counting in this example, where every redundant pair shares a term.

Example: artefact D has one element E1 and one figure F1. The panel has models M1 and M2, and each completes one schema-valid run on E1 for F1. Each run returns p = 0.1 and is decided no under SLP.24, assuming SLP.24 maps 0.1 to no. Since that rule is not given, the example can equally be built from whatever p values SLP.24 decides as no. No request fails the schema and no run is missing, so the verification is complete. Because every run of every panel model is decided no, E1 is decided as no defect. E1 then breaks no figure, the unweighted sum of violations over all figures is 0, and D is impeccable, satisfying a's 'if and only if'. Statement a governs how violations are counted and summed. Statement b governs how runs decide whether an element is a defect. Nothing in one forbids anything in the other. a's silence on escalated elements or incomplete verifications is not a conflict.

The two statements cover different matters. a sets how slop is counted: each element counts in every figure it breaks, the total is an unweighted sum over all figures, and an artefact is impeccable exactly when that sum is zero. b sets how contradiction is judged before a logic is chosen: each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone, with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0 with the hash-identified template. The reply is contradiction, compatible or refer; a refer is escalated to the user; a schema or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete and is not a decision. Neither statement constrains the other's counting or procedure. Example satisfying both: an artefact has two elements that both use the term 'Figure'. That pair alone is sent to the specified model at temperature 0 with the hash-identified template and the glossary definition of 'Figure'. The schema-valid reply is compatible, with an example satisfying both elements. No refer occurs and no failure occurs. No element breaks any figure, so the unweighted sum of violations over all figures is zero and the artefact is impeccable. Every clause of a and b holds at once.

A defines how slop is counted: unweighted, with each element counted once per figure it breaks, and impeccable meaning a total of zero. B says the statistical verifier is tested against a corpus whose slop is already known. These fit together. Example: the corpus holds document D1, where element e1 breaks figures F1 and F2 and element e2 breaks F1, giving slop 3 by A's rule. It also holds document D2 with no violations, so slop 0 and D2 is impeccable. The fixed decision question is sent N times to the fixed models for each document. The resulting probabilities are compared with the known values (3 and 0), the same way any candidate would be scored. A's counting rule supplies the 'known slop' that B needs, and B places no requirement on how slop is counted.

The two statements govern different things. (a) defines how an artefact's slop is counted. (b) defines how a candidate detector is scored against a true set of violations. Both can hold in one setup. Take corpus K1 = {document D} with elements e1 and e2, and figures F1 and F2. Element e1 breaks F1 and F2; e2 breaks F1. Under (a), e1 counts in both figures it breaks, so slop(D) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 with no weights, and D is not impeccable. The true violation set, identified by figure, element and detail, is {(F1,e1,x), (F2,e1,y), (F1,e2,z)}. Take corpus K2 = {document E} with no violations: slop 0, so E is impeccable, and its true set is empty. Candidate C outputs exactly those three triples for D and nothing for E. Its symmetric difference is 0 on both corpora, and two runs produce identical output. So C meets (b)'s necessary conditions for passing, and every clause of (a) also holds. The example avoids one open point: whether an element breaking the same figure in two different details counts once (a) or twice (b).

The two statements cover different periods. b applies only 'until a logic is chosen'. a describes how things work once elements are written as formulas in a decidable logic, with description logics as the candidate. Example: today no logic has been chosen. Redundancy is judged by a versioned yes/no question with typed yes/no criteria, sent via the OpenRouter Decisions API to google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. A model whose output repeats exactly runs once; any other runs three times. Only elements sharing a term are compared. Later a description logic is adopted and elements are formalised. From then on, a contradiction is a minimal unsatisfiable subset and an element is redundant when the rest entails it. That judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded. Running some models once and others three times fits the definition's N, which can differ per model. No clause of either statement is violated.

Example: elements are written as formulas in a decidable description logic such as OWL 2 DL. A reasoner lists each minimal unsatisfiable subset as a contradiction and flags any element the rest entails as redundant. These results are computed once at formalisation and recorded, so this judgement has moved out of verification, satisfying a. Verification still runs a panel of two models on each element for a remaining criterion, such as 'is this element ambiguous?'. Each run returns p and is decided under SLP.24. An element with all runs decided yes is a defect, one with all runs decided no is not, and a mixed result is escalated to the user. A schema-failing request is logged as a failure, not a run, and a missing run marks the verification incomplete, satisfying b. Statement a only moves the contradiction and redundancy judgement out of verification. It does not forbid model-run verification of other criteria, and b never says its runs judge contradiction or redundancy. (If 'the judgement' in a were read as all verification judgement, b would clash, but in context it refers to contradiction and redundancy.)

The two statements describe different phases. a describes the target state: once elements are written as formulas in a decidable logic, contradiction is a minimal unsatisfiable subset, redundancy is entailment by the rest, and the judgement is made once at formalisation and recorded. By calling description logics 'the candidate', a also implies the logic has not yet been chosen. b governs only the period 'until a logic is chosen'. Example: today no logic is chosen, so each pair of elements sharing a term is sent alone with the relevant glossary definitions to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0, using the hash-identified template. The reply is contradiction, compatible or refer; a refer goes to the user, and a schema or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete. Later a description logic is adopted, elements are formalised, and contradiction and redundancy are computed and recorded at formalisation. Every clause of both statements holds in this sequence.

The answer depends on what statement a's 'moves from verification to formalisation, where it is made once' rules out.

Reading 1 (compatible): a only means the contradiction and redundancy judgement is no longer repeated at every verification. Here 'once' means once per unchanged input. Example: an element's text is formalised into a description-logic formula, perhaps by models using N samples with k agreement. That judgement is recorded with the input hash, template hash, models, N and k. A decidable reasoner then counts minimal unsatisfiable subsets and entailed elements. A later verification reads the record and re-formalises only when a hash changes. This satisfies every clause of both statements.

Reading 2 (contradiction): a means verification no longer makes this judgement at all, and that it is made exactly once. b says a new verification 'judges again when a hash changes', so verification itself repeats the judgement. That conflicts with both 'moves from verification' and 'made once'.

Scope also matters. b's 'each judgement' may cover only other verification judgements, which avoids the conflict. Or it may include a's contradiction and redundancy judgement, which brings the conflict back. The pair does not settle which reading is meant.

Example: the elements of each artefact are written as formulas in a decidable description logic such as ALC. Formalisation is done once and recorded. A contradiction is reported as a minimal unsatisfiable subset, and an element is reported as redundant when the remaining formulas entail it. The candidate under test is an evaluator built on this. Its detected violations, each identified by figure, element and detail, exactly match the true sets on every corpus, so the symmetric-difference error is zero. Being deterministic, it gives identical output on two runs and passes. Statement a fixes how contradiction and redundancy are defined and which logic is used. Statement b fixes how a candidate is scored and when it passes. No clause of one restricts the other. 'Candidate' may mean a candidate logic in a and a candidate evaluator in b, but the example satisfies both statements either way.

The two statements cover different parts of one process. a sets up the verifier, the panel, the run counts and which elements are compared. b sets out what each run returns and how runs are combined. Example: no logic is chosen yet. Elements E1 and E2 both contain the term 'Verification', so they may be compared for redundancy. A versioned yes-or-no question with typed yes and no criteria goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to the pinned panel. google/gemini-decision-1 repeats its output exactly, so it is run once and returns p=0.92. perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2 does not repeat exactly, so it is run three times and returns p=0.88, 0.91 and 0.95. No request fails the schema, so all four runs count and none is missing. Suppose SLP.24 decides each of these p values as yes. (SLP.24 is not defined in the pair; the example only assumes it turns each p into yes or no.) Every run of every panel model is then yes, so E1 is decided as a redundancy defect.
