This satisfies every clause of a and b. Had any run been decided no, the element would be escalated to the user, which also conflicts with nothing in a.

The statements cover different checks: a covers redundancy and b covers contradiction. Both apply until a logic is chosen. Example: a fixed versioned yes/no redundancy question with typed yes and no criteria goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Gemini repeats its output exactly, so it is run once; pplx is run three times. Only elements that share a term are compared. Separately, each term-sharing pair is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt uses the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by its SHA-256 hash, plus the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses. Replies are contradiction (naming the requirements that cannot hold together), compatible (with a satisfying example) or refer. A refer is escalated to the user. A schema failure or transport failure leaves the verification incomplete and is not a decision. Both are restricted to term-sharing elements, so even if a's restriction were read as applying to all comparisons, b still satisfies it. Nothing in a requires contradiction to use a statistical verifier, and nothing in b forbids one for redundancy.

Statement a describes how the interim statistical verifier is built and run. Statement b adds that this verifier is tested against a corpus with known slop, as candidates are. Nothing in a forbids evaluating the verifier, so the two fit together. Example: before any logic is chosen, redundancy is judged by verifier question v1. It has typed yes and no criteria and goes through the OpenRouter Decisions API to pinned google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Gemini's output repeats exactly, so it is run once. pplx is not repeat-exact, so it is run three times. Only elements sharing a term are compared. The same verifier is also run on a corpus of artefacts whose slop (figure violations) is known in advance, and its judgements are scored against those known labels, just as each candidate is scored.

The two statements govern different things. Statement a says how redundancy is judged until a logic is chosen. Statement b says how a candidate is scored and when it passes. Neither forbids what the other requires. Example: no logic has been chosen yet. Redundancy is judged by verifier question v1, with typed yes and no criteria, sent through the OpenRouter Decisions API to google/gemini-decision-1 and perplexity/pplx-decider-v1.2. Gemini's output repeats exactly, so it is run once. Pplx's output varies, so it is run three times. Only elements E1 and E2 share the term 'corpus', so only that pair is compared. Separately, candidate C is tested on a single corpus whose true violation set is {(redundancy, E1, 'restates E2')}. C detects exactly that set, so the symmetric difference is empty and the error is 0. C gives identical output on two runs, so it passes. Even if the verifier were itself treated as a candidate, b would only make it fail under some outcomes; nothing in either statement forces the two to conflict.

The answer depends on whether a's procedure also governs the contradiction checks in b. Separate-scope reading: a sets the general rule for deciding element-level defects from panel runs, and b sets an interim rule for contradiction checks on pairs of elements ('until a logic is chosen'). On this reading both can hold. Example: a's panel answers some yes/no quality question about each element; each run returns p, is decided under SLP.24 and is aggregated as a requires. Meanwhile each term-sharing pair is sent alone with the relevant glossary definitions to claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0 using the hashed template, and gets a three-way reply. Even on this reading, schema failures agree: under a a failed request is not a run, so the run is missing and verification is incomplete, which matches b. Shared-scope reading: a's rules also cover contradiction judgement. Then every run must return a probability p that the answer is yes and be decided yes or no under SLP.24, while b requires the reply to be exactly one of three labels. Also, b's contradiction outcome must name the conflicting requirements and its compatible outcome must give an example. A single probability with a yes/no outcome does not fit a three-way labelled reply. On this reading the two reply formats appear unable to hold together. A one-model panel would satisfy a's panel requirement, so model count is not the obstacle; the reply format is. The pair does not say which scope is intended, and SLP.24 is undefined, so neither result can be established.

Example: element E is judged by panel models M1 and M2, with N=3 and k=2. All six runs return a p, and each is decided 'yes' under SLP.24. No request fails the schema and no run is missing, so E is decided a defect and the verification is complete. This judgement is recorded with the input hash, the template hash, the models, N and k. A later verification reads the record and finds both hashes unchanged, so it does not judge again and reuses the recorded runs. No runs are missing in that verification either. Statement a governs how runs are decided and aggregated; statement b governs recording and when to re-judge. Nothing in either forbids the other.

The two statements govern different things, so both can hold. a covers how panel-model runs decide whether an element is a defect. b covers how a candidate is scored against true violations. Example: the panel is one model M, and the only element is E1 in artefact A. M runs twice on E1 with no schema failures and no missing runs, so verification is complete. Each run returns p and is decided under SLP.24; take the outcome for the chosen p to be yes in both runs. Every run is yes, so E1 is a defect. If SLP.24 never yields yes, take p values it decides as no instead, so every run is no and E1 is no defect. The true violation set below then becomes empty. Candidate C is run twice on the single corpus {A}. Each run outputs the violation set {(figure F, element E1, detail d)}, which equals the true set. The symmetric difference is empty, so error is 0 on every corpus, and the two outputs are identical. C passes. Every clause of a and b is satisfied.

Example: two elements share a term. The pair is sent alone, with the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses, to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt uses the template calibration/contradiction-v2/text.txt, identified by SHA-256 hash H. The reply is 'compatible' and gives an example satisfying both elements. This judgement is recorded with the hash of its input, template hash H, models = [anthropic/claude-opus-5.5], N = 1 and k = 1. A later verification reads the record, finds both hashes unchanged and does not judge again. If a hash had changed, it would re-judge. A 'refer' reply would be recorded the same way and escalated to the user. A schema failure or transport failure is not an assessment, so it is not a judgement. Nothing is recorded, and the verification stays incomplete, as (a) requires. (b)'s plural 'models' and its N and k are satisfied by a one-model list and N = k = 1. Nothing in (a) forbids recording or reusing judgements.

The two statements cover different things. Statement a sets out how contradiction is judged until a logic is chosen. Statement b defines how a candidate is scored and when it passes. Neither requirement limits the other. Example: before any logic is chosen, each pair of elements that share a term is sent alone to anthropic/claude-opus-5.5 at temperature 0. The prompt uses the template identified by its SHA-256 hash and includes the glossary definitions of the terms either element uses. Every reply fits the schema: contradiction with the named requirements, compatible with an example, or refer. Every refer is escalated to the user. Schema failures and transport failures leave the verification incomplete and are not counted as decisions. Separately, a candidate is run on every corpus. Its detected set of violations, each identified by figure, element and detail, exactly equals the true set, so the symmetric difference is zero. A second run produces identical output. That candidate passes. All clauses of both statements hold together.

Example: a hidden hold-out of 50 artefacts includes 20 with known slop (seeded figure violations). The statistical verifier sends its fixed decision question N times to fixed models on each artefact. A script hidden from all candidates compares the verifier's outputs with the truth labels and computes its score. Other candidates are scored the same way. No candidate, including the verifier if it counts as one, can read the truth labels, the clean corpus, the hold-out or the script. Being evaluated against a corpus does not require reading it, so every clause of a and b is met.

Statement a only says the statistical verifier is evaluated on a known-slop corpus the same way any candidate is. Statement b gives that evaluation: error is the symmetric difference between detected and true violations, each keyed by (figure, element, detail), and passing requires zero error on every corpus plus identical output on two runs. A concrete case satisfies both. Take one corpus whose true slop set is {(F1, E7, 'repeated hedge')}. The verifier sends its fixed question N times to fixed models and thresholds the resulting probabilities. On both runs it reports exactly {(F1, E7, 'repeated hedge')}. The symmetric difference is empty, so error is 0, and the two runs match, so it passes. Nothing in either statement requires the verifier to pass. Its sampling could make it fail the identical-output test, and that would still be consistent with both statements, because being evaluated like any candidate includes the possibility of failing.

Example: there are three corpora: a training corpus the candidates may read, a clean corpus, and a hold-out. The truth files, the clean corpus and the hold-out are stored where no candidate can open them, and the scoring script is hidden. The hidden script runs each candidate on every corpus, passing it one artefact at a time. Each detected violation is recorded as a (figure, element, detail) triple. The script computes the symmetric difference between the detected set and the true set; for the clean corpus the true set is empty. One candidate outputs exactly the true triples on every corpus, gives the same output on both runs, and so passes. A candidate that misses one violation has error 1 and fails. Statement a restricts what candidates can access. Statement b defines the error and the pass rule. Neither requires a candidate to read the truth or the script. The definitions themselves expect a candidate to be tested on a corpus hidden from it (the hold-out), so being run on the hold-out is not reading it.

b is a question, so it asserts nothing that could conflict with a. At most it presupposes that quality belongs either to the result or to the task-result relation. Example: a user delegates a comparison loop under its own agreement, which settles how the group communicates before work starts. The loop runs autonomously, and the user validates its output at the end. Meanwhile someone asks whether that output's quality lies in the result itself or in how well it fits the task. Every clause of a holds, and b's question and its presupposition stay open and consistent with a.

Both items are questions, so neither asserts anything that could clash. Their presuppositions can all hold together. (a) presupposes that quality belongs either to the result or to the task–result relation. (b) presupposes that quality has measurement dimensions and that product quality can be told apart from process quality. Concrete example: a framework treats quality as the relation between a task (e.g., a problem) and what is produced for it. It measures that relation along dimensions such as correctness, completeness and efficiency. It then separates product quality (how well the final result meets the task's criteria) from process quality (how well the work steps meet criteria for pursuing the task). This framework answers (a) with 'the relation' and answers (b) with those dimensions and that split, while staying consistent with the given definitions of Task and Quality.
